- Insert- or erase-heavy workloads. In the same benchmark CSVs on the 3990X, insert-with-reserve at n=10^7 cost about 2,517 ns per element vs 193 ns for std::unordered_map. Erase+insert at n=150,000 cost 2,176 ns vs 59 ns, and at 10^7 it timed out. An insert that breaks perfectness re-places its bucket or rebuilds the whole table.
- Very small tables on x86 and very large hit-lookup tables at default load factor. ska::flat_hash_map + std::hash beat it below about 1,000 elements on the 3990X, and in the 2023 rerun again when data fit in L2 and once it exceeded L3. For large-n misses, absl::flat_hash_map beat DynamicFphMap in the 2022 data.
- Key sets you cannot vet. If the seed search fails, which duplicate keys passed to Build()/InsertNoDuplicated() or poorly distributed hashes can cause, construction throws std::invalid_argument ('timeout when try to build fph map'), or calls std::abort with exceptions disabled. With 64-bit hashes of long keys (strings), the README warns collisions become likely beyond about 10^9 keys.
- Code that needs std::unordered_map's reference stability, node handles (extract/merge), insert_or_assign, or stateful hashers and allocators. None of these are provided.
- Maturity-sensitive deployments. The header logic has not changed since August 2023, the project has 55 stars, and its own CI docs admit an unfixed defect that trips an assert at -O0 and becomes heap corruption under -DNDEBUG, plus a known defect that crashes on x86-64 but passes on arm64. No issue describes either one.

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only); optional CMake INTERFACE target fph::fph_table via add_subdirectory · C++17. CI compiles with GCC and Clang at C++17/20/23 on Ubuntu 24.04 (GCC 13, Clang 18) and Apple clang on macOS 15. The README says MSVC compiles but it is not in CI. The published benchmarks used GCC 10.2 and Apple clang 13.1.6. · Portable scalar C++ with no SIMD intrinsics. CI covers Linux x86-64, Linux arm64 and macOS arm64 (LP64). Windows/MSVC compiles per the README but is untested.

**Vs siblings:** Pick fph-table over the constexpr-oriented siblings (constexpr-phf, ConstexprCore/perfect_hash) and frozen's small fixed tables when keys are only known at run time, number from thousands to millions, or need occasional insert/erase behind an unordered_map-style API. Pick it over cxxmph's mph_map for integer keys: fph reports 2-7x over std::unordered_map, while cxxmph claims 10-50% on large URL-string sets.

**Gotchas:**
- The const operator[] on DynamicFphMap is noexcept and skips the key check (it calls GetPointerNoCheck). For an absent key it silently returns another element's value or reads an unconstructed slot. Use find() or at() unless the key is known to be present.
- SeedHash and KeyEqual are static constexpr members, so they must be stateless and constexpr default-constructible, and a hasher instance passed to the constructor is ignored. Slot and bucket storage use default-constructed rebound allocators, so stateful allocators are not honored.
- Empty slots in the Dynamic variants hold copies of a randomly generated filler key. Every unused slot therefore holds a constructed key (a random short string for std::string keys), and custom key types must supply a RandomKeyGenerator. MetaFph* avoids this with its metadata byte.
- Pointers and references can be invalidated by any insert (bucket re-placement or full rebuild), not only by rehash. begin() moves to the most recently inserted or erased element, so iteration order shifts after every modification. The default max_load_factor is 0.6 (settable up to 0.98) over power-of-two slot counts, and the default BucketParamType=uint32_t caps capacity at 2^31 slots.

**Status:** Header logic frozen since August 2023, but the author added an Apache-2.0 license and an extensive CI suite (compile matrix, ctest, ASan/UBSan, asm/callgrind lookup gates) in August 2026, so it is lightly maintained, and at two self-contained headers of about 4k lines each it is easy to vendor and pin.

[repo](https://github.com/renzibei/fph-table) · [benchmark](https://github.com/renzibei/hashtable-bench)

##### frozen  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++14 constexpr immutable set/map/unordered_map built on compile-time perfect hashing; beats std::unordered_map on fixed key sets.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map (arXiv 2602.22506 demos); std::set and std::unordered_set in the author's first-party 2018 Quarkslab microbenchmark — The static_maps preprint (arXiv 2602.22506) timed construction plus lookup for frozen::unordered_map (frozen::basic_string keys, built at compile time) against std::unordered_map<std::string_view> (libstdc++, built at runtime inside the timed region). Setup: g++ 15.2.1 -O3 -march=native on a Core i5-1240P laptop. Results: 44.9 vs 89.6 us for 1,024 individually timed lookups in an 84-key map (~2.0x); 1365.5 vs 1746.8 us translating 65,536 codons through a 64-key map (~1.28x); 15804.5 vs 21228.1 us for 258,688 value updates in a 4,042-key map (~1.34x).

**Independent measurement:** On a 92-key C++ keyword set (200k words, 1:8 keyword:identifier) frozen::unordered_map took 18.888 ns per lookup vs 5.322 ns for developer source's compile-time perfect hash table (3.55x slower; 3.5-3.7x across runs) and 29.168 ns for std::unordered_map (frozen 1.54x faster, derived). (developer source, private repo; gcc 13.3.0 -O2 -march=native, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-02-libraries)

**How:** unordered_* uses a two-level perfect hash (not minimal) in the hash-and-displace style of Steve Hanov's 'Throw away the keys', built entirely in constexpr. Keys are seed-hashed into M buckets, where M is the next power of two at or above N (doubled below 32 keys). Buckets are processed largest first. A singleton bucket stores its item index directly in table G. A larger bucket gets a per-bucket seed, found by random search with minstd_rand, that puts all its items into free slots of table H. A lookup is one hash into G, at most one more seeded hash into H, then a single key comparison: no probing, no chains, no heap. frozen::set and frozen::map are sorted arrays searched by a fully unrolled branchless binary search.

**Use it when:**
- Lookup tables whose key set is fixed at build time: keyword/command/opcode dispatch, enum<->string, symbol tables, HTML entities (all shipped as examples). Tens to a few thousand keys.
- You need lookups in constant expressions (static_assert, template arguments, constexpr functions), or want constant-key lookups folded away entirely.
- You want no static-initialization cost and no heap: declare constexpr or constinit and the table goes into the binary. FROZEN_NO_EXCEPTIONS (or -fno-exceptions) turns at()'s throw into std::abort for embedded builds.
- Keys are fixed but values change at runtime, like the preprint's 4,042-key ticker->price table (~1.34x vs std::unordered_map). Use a constinit map and write through at() or find()->second.
- Ordered lookups (lower_bound/upper_bound, sorted iteration) over immutable data, where frozen::map/set replace a node-based std::map/std::set with a sorted array.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys are only known at runtime, or the set changes: there is no insert, erase or rehash. Use a runtime hash map, or a runtime-built PHF such as fph-table or cmph.
- Large key sets. In the preprint, frozen took 21.1 s to compile the 4,042-key demo vs 1.5 s for std::unordered_map. Big tables hit constexpr step limits (-fconstexpr-steps / -fconstexpr-ops-limit), and issue #76 (open) reports VS2017 failing at 500 entries.
- Raw lookup throughput is the goal. static_maps ran at 45-97% of frozen's time in the same preprint, and the ConstexprCore/perfect_hash benchmark shows frozen::unordered_map at 0.16 vs 1.08 billion queries/s.
- Long string keys on a hot path. The default string hash is a byte-at-a-time FNV-1a-style loop and can run twice per lookup (G then H), so cost grows with key length.
- MSVC with warnings-as-errors: the constexpr hash triggers C4307 'integral constant overflow' warnings (#68, #178). Also, wasm32 has an open, unreproduced report of failed lookups (#198).

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only) · C++14. README: Clang 5+, GCC 6+ (slow constexpr), VS2017; GCC 5 unsupported. CI builds GCC 10-13, Clang 13/14/16, AppleClang and MSVC at C++14/17/2a. std::string_view keys need C++17, constinit needs C++20. CMake 3.10+ for the optional install/find_package path. · any (portable C++, no intrinsics). CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows; the Windows job builds but does not run the tests. One open, unconfirmed wasm32 lookup bug report (#198).

**Vs siblings:** Pick frozen over ConstexprCore/perfect_hash or constexpr-phf (Kronuz) when you want the long-established, C++14-compatible option with a full std-like container family, including ordered map/set with lower_bound. Pick those (or static_maps) when lookup throughput matters most: ConstexprCore's benchmark has frozen::unordered_map at 0.16 vs 1.08 billion queries/s. Unlike the gperf-style generators (triehash, strager/perfect-hash-tables), frozen needs no external build step.

**Gotchas:**
- Duplicate keys are not reliably caught. The Step 1.5 check in bits/pmh.h compares items[0] with items[i] rather than with the members of each bucket, so most duplicates make the seed search spin. Under constexpr that shows up as a constexpr step-limit error; a map built at runtime loops forever (#181).
- A map that is neither constexpr nor constinit may be built at runtime, with the seed search running at static-init or first use. Use constinit (C++20), as examples/value_modification.cpp does, to force compile-time construction and get an error when it fails.
- There is no operator[]. at() throws std::out_of_range, or calls std::abort when exceptions are off. Custom hashers must accept a seed and should be close to pairwise-independent; a weak hash does not break correctness but makes compiles slow or exceed constexpr limits.
- The default key type frozen::string is a non-owning pointer+length view. std::string_view keys work only if you include the internal header frozen/bits/elsa_std.h, which the README does not mention. The version macros read 1.1.1 and the CMake project reads 1.1.0, while the latest tag is 1.2.0.

**Status:** The README says the library is in maintenance mode: it still merges cleanups (last commit 2026-09-23; 1.2.0 tagged 2024-06). It is Apache-2.0 and header-only, so you can copy include/frozen into your tree or install via CMake.

[repo](https://github.com/serge-sans-paille/frozen) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.22506)

##### hashify  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust proc-macro that compiles fixed byte-string keyword sets into perfect-hash lookups; beats string `match` and the phf crate.

**Beats:** switch/if-else chains — The author's criterion benchmark (benches/lookup.rs, Apple M5 Max, Rust 1.98, default cargo bench profile at opt-level 3) times hashify map! against a Rust `match` with one string arm per key on five real key sets. Results run from 0.68 vs 1.34 ns (9 HTTP methods, hits) to 1.84 vs 39.8 ns (2125 HTML entities, random with half near-misses), about 1.25x-21.6x, plus 4.1x-12.6x over phf 0.14 CHD and 3.2x-8.8x over phf ptrhash; there is no C++ std or gperf comparison, and nobody has reproduced the results independently.

**How:** Keys of up to 16 bytes are packed into two u64 words (the first and last 8 bytes, which can overlap) plus the length. A hit is then confirmed with three integer compares, with no memcmp and no pointer chase. Longer keys go in a second table and are compared 8 bytes at a time. Up to 16 keys become a gperf --switch style decision tree on the length and one byte (or the XOR of two bytes). 17-64 keys get a collision-free power-of-two table with a searched seed (one multiply, a shift and a load). Larger sets get a PtrHash/PHast-style minimal perfect hash with one 8-bit pilot per bucket, found by a cuckoo-like eviction search. The hash is a cheap multiply-and-fold of the key words rather than the SipHash-1-3 that phf uses, and 32-bit targets get separate tables built from a 32-bit hash.

**Use it when:**
- Rust protocol or format parsers that dispatch on a fixed keyword set known at compile time. The benchmarked sets are HTTP methods, IMAP commands, Sieve keywords, charset names and HTML entities.
- Replacing a string `match` with more than ~100 arms. `match` measured 7.5-7.8 ns per random lookup at 128-149 keys and 25-40 ns at 2125 keys, against about 1.8-2 ns for hashify.
- Replacing phf_map!/phf_set! when the keys are literals. It was 4.1x-12.6x faster than phf 0.14 CHD in the author's benchmark, including the synthetic sets of 10k and 100k keys.
- Miss-heavy input such as tokenizing untrusted text. Half the probes in the random workload are one-bit-off misses, and hashify stays at about 1.0-2.2 ns per lookup.
- no_std, no-alloc or unsafe-forbidding code. The generated code uses only `core` paths, never allocates (tested with a counting allocator) and compiles under #![forbid(unsafe_code)].

**Skip it when:**
- C or C++ code. It is a Rust proc macro with no C ABI and no standalone code-generator output.
- Keys known only at runtime, built programmatically, or named by `const` items or enum variants. Only literal tokens are accepted ('unsupported key expression', issue #1), and there is no build.rs/codegen API (issue #2 is still open).
- Small sets of up to ~26 keys, where a plain `match` stays within 2x (1.34-2.51 ns) and needs no dependency.
- Very large key sets in a crate you rebuild often. The macro re-runs on every compile, incremental builds included, and 1,000,000 keys add about 24 s (15 s with build-override opt-level 3). A `fnc_map!` with 10,000 arms costs about 4 s of extra LLVM time in release builds.
- Case-insensitive matching beyond ASCII. The `_ignore_case` variants fold only A-Z, and all other bytes must match exactly.

**Integration:** crate (procedural macro) · none at runtime; syn 3.0, quote and proc-macro2 at build time · Rust 1.88 (Cargo.toml rust-version), edition 2024 · any Rust target; no architecture-specific code; 32-bit targets get separate 32-bit-hash tables via cfg(target_pointer_width)

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling is C++ (qlibs mph, constexpr-phf, frozen, ConstexprCore/perfect_hash, triehash and the other gperf alternatives), so pick hashify only when the lookup lives in Rust. There it fills the role constexpr-phf or mph fill in C++, and like constexpr-phf it is benchmarked directly against the switch/match baseline; for C++ code, use a sibling.

**Gotchas:**
- Integer keys are matched against their big-endian bytes (`1u16` matches [0, 1]). `map!` values are stored in a `static`, so they must be constant expressions.
- 0.3.0 (2026-09-23) was a rewrite. The 0.2 `tiny_map!`/`tiny_set!` macros are gone, and the algorithm changed from FNV-1a + PTHash to the current scheme, so 0.2 users have to migrate. Separately, 0.2 releases before 0.2.8 produced non-reproducible builds (issue #4).
- Keep big lookups in their own crate and set `[profile.release.build-override] opt-level = 3`. Cargo compiles proc macros without optimization by default, which slows table construction (24.07 s vs 15.24 s at 1M keys).
- Table construction can fail with the compile error 'failed to resolve hash collision' once its seed and load-factor retries run out. Large or hard key sets may get up to 5% spare slots instead of a strictly minimal table.

**Status:** Actively maintained by Stalwart Labs: v0.3.1 reached crates.io on 2026-09-24 under MIT OR Apache-2.0, the crate has ~2.67M downloads and Stalwart's own mail-parser, mail-auth and sieve-rs crates depend on it, but the 0.3 rewrite is only days old and the crate can be reused only from Rust projects.

[repo](https://github.com/stalwartlabs/hashify) · [benchmark](https://github.com/stalwartlabs/hashify/blob/main/README.md)

##### mph (qlibs)  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier A`

C++20 compile-time perfect-hash lookup built on BMI2 pext; 2.4-10x lower latency than std::unordered_map on 5-100-key string sets.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map (std::hash), std::map, boost::unordered_flat_map (Boost 1.85), frozen::unordered_map, gperf, if-else and switch-case chains — In the author's nanobench run, lookups were random hits drawn from sets of 5-100 strings of 1-8 bytes. It used clang++ and g++ with -O3 -mbmi2 and libstdc++ on the g++ run; no CPU model or compiler versions are given. mph measured 1.4-7.2 ns per lookup, against 5.3-25.4 ns for std::unordered_map (with boost::hash) and 7.7-13.1 ns for gperf. The lead over gperf shrinks to 1.3-2.2x on the variable-length sets. The harness calls the v2-era mph::hash/mph::fixed_string API, which the current header no longer has, so the tables predate the current lookup/find code.

**How:** All table construction happens at compile time. For very small sets, lookup uses a PCG generator to search for a multiplier such that (key*magic)>>shift picks a bit-field out of one 32/64-bit constant, so the lookup is a multiply, a shift and a mask with no memory access. Otherwise it greedily finds the smallest bit mask that keeps every key unique; at run time, BMI2 PEXT packs those bits into a dense index into a 2^popcount(mask) table, and find does one full-key compare (a cmov by default). Strings up to 16 bytes are loaded as one integer (memcpy plus BZHI to trim the length), so there is no per-character hashing or probe loop, and find on more than 64 entries does a single std::experimental::simd bucket compare.

**Use it when:**
- Hot-path mapping of a fixed set of short keys known at build time: keyword or command parsing, string_to_enum/enum_to_string, ticker-symbol or message-type dispatch (the README examples).
- Sets of a few keys up to about a thousand. The README latency tables cover 5-100 string keys; the author's plot-only benchmark goes to 1024 keys.
- Strings of 8 bytes or fewer, and ideally 4 or fewer (the FAQ says a smaller maximum length gives a smaller table and one fewer instruction), or integer keys as u32/u64.
- x86-64 with fast PEXT (Intel Haswell+ or AMD Zen3+ per the FAQ), built with -mbmi2 or -march=native.
- Inputs that are always in the set: mph::lookup (or find<100>) skips the key compare and, for tiny integer sets, compiles to 3-5 instructions (README asm).

**Skip it when:**
- Keys that are only known, or change, at run time. There is no insert, erase or iteration; the table is generated at compile time.
- Long keys. Keys must fit in 128 bits (16 bytes), or lookup/find are removed by SFINAE and you must write your own fallback policy (issues #5 and #6 are still open). The mask search also looks at only the low 64 bits (mask<u64>), so keys that share their first 8 bytes can fail (issue #3).
- MSVC or libc++. The requirements list only GCC 12+ and Clang 15+, and the header uses GCC/Clang builtins. Open PR #19 reports that main does not compile with libc++'s partial <experimental/simd>.
- Large sets. The FAQ says it handles thousands of keys, not millions; build time grows with size and can hit constexpr step limits.
- CPUs with slow PEXT (AMD Zen2 takes 18 cycles per the FAQ) or non-x86 targets. Both use the software pext fallback, and no run-time numbers are published for it.

**Integration:** header-only · none (optional <experimental/simd> from libstdc++, which find needs for sets of more than 64 entries) · C++20; GCC 12+ or Clang 15+ (README). A C++20 module wrapper, mph.cppm, is also provided. · x86-64 is the target (BMI2 optional but recommended; AVX2/AVX-512 used through std::experimental::simd); other targets, including arm-none-eabi since issue #14, use a software pext fallback; GCC/Clang only

**Vs siblings:** Pick mph over frozen or gperf when your keys are integers, enums or strings of 8 bytes or fewer on x86-64 with BMI2 and per-lookup latency matters most. The author's plots put it below frozen, gperf and boost::unordered_flat_map up to 1024 keys, and there is no head-to-head with Kronuz constexpr-phf or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash. Pick frozen instead for C++14, MSVC, longer strings or a container API; pick gperf or triehash for long string keys or generated C code.

**Gotchas:**
- mph::lookup returns an arbitrary value for a key that is not in the set. Use mph::find for untrusted input. find<100> (probability = 100) also skips the compare, so it behaves the same way.
- The header runs its self-tests as static_asserts every time you include it; define -DNTEST to skip them. Large sets can hit 'constexpr evaluation hit maximum step limit'; raise -fconstexpr-ops-limit (GCC) or -fconstexpr-steps (Clang).
- Without <experimental/simd>, find only accepts sets of 64 entries or fewer (requires-clause). Sets above 64 entries use SIMD buckets sized to the native register width.
- Main has an untagged change made after the v5.0.5 tag (PR #18, July 2025), still in the v5_0_5 inline namespace. The change narrows the probe key to the 32/64-bit mask type before find compares it with the full stored key. From reading the code (not compiled), keys longer than 4 bytes whose mask fits in 32 bits may stop matching, and no self-test covers this case. Pin tag v5.0.5 or test your key set.

**Status:** Stale: the last tagged release is v5.0.5 (Jan 2025), the last commit is a July 2025 community PR, and a libc++ build fix (PR #19) has been unmerged since Sept 2025. It is MIT-licensed, a single header with no dependencies, and easy to vendor; pin v5.0.5.

[repo](https://github.com/qlibs/mph) · [benchmark](https://qlibs.github.io/mph/perfect_hashing)

##### phashtable (gsauthof)  `C`  `BSL-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Tiny C/C++ two-level perfect hash index, built at startup, that flattens worst-case lookup latency versus std::unordered_map.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map — The author's Google Benchmark code hammers each of 2,776 ISINs in turn against gms::Phash_Table and libstdc++ std::unordered_map<const char*, uint32_t> (custom hash/equality functors), keeping each key's best of 3 pinned runs. With SDBM the slowest key costs 44 vs 61 ns on an Atom C3758 (g++ -O3 -march=goldmont-plus) and 12 vs 34 ns on a Xeon Gold 6246 (GCC 9, RHEL 7, 4.1 GHz), about 1.4x and 2.8x lower, though unordered_map's fastest keys still win (22 vs 43 and 9 vs 11 ns) and hot-key repetition means cache-miss latency was not measured.

**How:** It uses two-level perfect hashing in the style of the classic FKS scheme: a first-level table with n/2 buckets stores an offset, a secondary size (at most 255) and an 8-bit hash parameter per bucket. At build time, a per-bucket search over sizes and parameters makes every secondary table collision-free. Both levels map hashes to slots with Lemire's fast-range multiply-shift instead of modulo, and the default hash is SDBM with a parametrized multiplier (65599 + param). Every lookup runs two hash calls, two multiply-shifts and two table loads with no probing or chaining, even when the bucket's parameter is 0, so that every key costs the same.

**Use it when:**
- The key set is fixed or reloaded wholesale (for example a daily instrument/ISIN master file), and rebuilding at startup or re-init is acceptable.
- Latency-sensitive paths where the slowest key matters. On the author's Xeon, the per-key cost stays at 11-12 ns, while std::unordered_map ranges from 9 to 34 ns depending on the key.
- Short, fixed-length string keys with a cheap hash (the benchmark uses 12-byte ISINs with SDBM), especially on low-end cores like Atom, where the hash cost dominates.
- Large runtime key sets where gperf is impractical. The README builds 1.4M ISINs into about 11.4 MB, and reports that gperf did not finish on that set.
- C code, or C++ code that wants a ~370-line BSL-1.0 source drop mapping keys to positions in an existing array.

**Skip it when:**
- The set changes incrementally: there is no insert or delete, and any change means a full rebuild.
- You care about the best case or the average. unordered_map's fastest keys beat it (22 vs 43 ns on Atom, 9 vs 11 ns on Xeon, both with SDBM), because every lookup pays for two hash calls.
- Memory is tight. The index alone costs about 8.1-8.6 bytes/key on top of your item array, vs about 5.33 for a 75%-full open-addressing index; cmph's CHD needs about 2 bits/key.
- Many lookups are for absent keys, or the key set is untrusted. Lookup always returns some index, and a bad hash or duplicate keys make the build fail (bucket overflow gives -2; no collision-free secondary table gives -3).
- You need a maintained, tested dependency. The repo has 12 commits from Oct-Nov 2020, no tests beyond one example program, and no CI.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the library (libc calloc/free/memset). The example program uses POSIX getline. The benchmark needs Google Benchmark, an external SipHash checkout (not vendored) and libstdc++ internals (std::_Hash_bytes). · C99 for phash_table.c/.h (compound literals, stdbool) and C++11 for the phash_table.hh wrapper. The published benchmarks were built with g++ -std=gnu++17 (GCC 9). · Portable C with no intrinsics or arch-specific code, so any platform should work. It was only measured on x86-64 Linux (Atom C3758 on Fedora 31, Xeon Gold 6246 on RHEL 7).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over frozen (compile-time constexpr keys) when the keys arrive at run time and number in the millions, and over cmph when you want a tiny BSL-1.0 C drop-in that returns your original array index with flat per-key cost and can accept about 8 bytes/key vs CHD's ~2 bits/key. Choose fph-table instead if you want a C++17, std::unordered_map-like container that allows occasional inserts.

**Gotchas:**
- Lookup never says 'not found'. It returns an index for any key, and absent keys can land on unfilled slots that hold 0. Always compare the key stored at that index, as bench.cc and test_hash_table.c do with memcmp.
- One callback signature does two jobs. Build calls hfn(items, i, param) and lookup calls hfn(key, 0, param), so you normally write two functions that must hash identically. Only the low 8 bits feed the second level, with parameters 0-23 and secondary tables of at most 255 slots.
- C++ wrapper pitfalls. A plain `gms::Phash_Table t;` in automatic storage leaves the pointers uninitialized (the defaulted constructor sits over a C struct), and the destructor then frees them. Move assignment overwrites without freeing the old tables. Use `{}` or construct with data.
- Edge cases are unchecked. With n = 1 the bucket count is n/2 = 0, and the build writes out of bounds. The build computes 2*n in uint32_t, which caps sets below 2^31 keys. The makefile's default target references pybind11 sources that are not in the repo, so compile phash_table.c yourself.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2020-11-22 (12 commits, no issues or PRs ever filed) but BSL-1.0 and about 370 lines in three files, so it is easy to vendor and audit; the last known-good compiler is GCC 9.

[repo](https://github.com/gsauthof/phashtable) · [benchmark](https://github.com/gsauthof/phashtable#measurements)

##### static_maps  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++23 consteval FKS perfect-hash unordered_map for compile-time keysets; 1.4-2.9x faster than std::unordered_map in three paper demos.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map — Per-run time (std::unordered_map built at run time plus lookups, vs static_maps built by the compiler) was 35.8 vs 89.6 µs for 1,024 lookups in an 84-key element table, 607.6 vs 1746.8 µs for 65,536 lookups in a 64-codon table, and 15,295 vs 21,228 µs for about 259k in-place updates in a 4,042-ticker table that the paper calls S&P 500 (2.5x, 2.9x and 1.4x, derived from paper data). The authors measured this in their arXiv preprint with g++ 15.2.1 (libstdc++ inferred), -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native, on an Intel Core i5-1240P laptop at real-time priority with ASLR off; no independent run exists.

**How:** It uses Fredman-Komlos-Szemeredi (FKS) two-level perfect hashing with multipliers found by a consteval xorshift64* search. The raw hash (DJB2 for string_view, identity for integers) is multiplied by k modulo the largest prime of a 16/32/64-bit SIZE_T and masked into a power-of-two primary table with 8-16 slots per key. A bucket with one key returns at once; a colliding bucket uses its own multiplier and a quadratic-size secondary table. Because the table is collision-free and sits in .rodata, `operator[]` does no key comparison, probing, heap access or run-time construction, and the factory picks the smallest SIZE_T that keeps truncated hashes distinct (adding an XOR salt if needed), with a compare-and-subtract modulo replacing `%` for 64-bit SIZE_T.

**Use it when:**
- Fixed string-to-value tables compiled into the binary (symbol, opcode, keyword, codon or ticker lookups) where every key is known at build time and std::unordered_map is only used as a read-mostly dictionary.
- Hot loops where run-time lookups dominate: the codon demo (64 keys, 65,536 lookups per run) showed the largest gain, about 2.9x over std::unordered_map and 2.2x over Frozen (derived from paper data).
- Programs that start often or must not allocate at startup: the compiler builds the table and places it in .rodata, so there is no construction cost or heap allocation at run time.
- Fixed key universe with changing values, where jitter matters: the 4,042-ticker update demo uses a constinit map with mutable values, and its run-time standard deviation was ±950.6 µs vs ±1660.8 µs for std::unordered_map.
- Code that already uses std::string_view keys, builds with a C++23 GCC 15 or Clang 21, and can accept much longer compile times for the tables involved.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys that are not known until run time, or keysets that change often: there is no insert or erase, and each keyset change is a recompile.
- Large keysets or tight build budgets: at 4,042 keys the build took 55.2 s vs 1.5 s for std::unordered_map, raised constexpr limits are required, and nothing larger than 4,042 keys was tested.
- Miss-heavy lookups or membership tests: there is no find, contains or count, operator[] returns an arbitrary value or throws for an absent key, and at() reports every miss by throwing std::out_of_range (after an internal throw and catch), which is slow when misses are common.
- Cache-constrained large tables: with the default DELTA_PRIMARY=8 each key gets 8-16 primary rows, each holding three SIZE_T fields in three separate arrays, so a lookup can touch several arrays plus the value array; the paper itself warns that a large delta stresses the CPU cache.
- Pre-C++23 toolchains, MSVC, -fno-exceptions builds, or teams that need a maintained project: other compilers are not documented, the lookup path uses throw/try/catch, and the code is a one-off figshare deposit whose only test suite belongs to the vendored Frozen.

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only; the vendored Frozen 1.1.1 copy is used only by the comparison demos) · C++23 (uses deducing this, std::views::zip/adjacent and constexpr std::vector). Tested only with GCC 15.2.1 and Clang 21.1.6; the paper says earlier working versions are unknown. GCC needs a raised -fconstexpr-ops-limit (and -fconstexpr-loop-limit for large keysets), Clang a raised -fconstexpr-steps, and the 4,042-key demo on Clang also needed -fexperimental-new-constant-interpreter. · any target with a C++23 GCC or Clang (benchmarked only on x86-64 Linux); the optional USING_UINT128 path needs __uint128_t; MSVC not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick static_maps over frozen when your keys are std::string_view (Frozen needs its own frozen::string type) and lookups dominate: in the paper's demos it beat the vendored Frozen 1.1.1 by 1.25x, 2.25x and 1.03x (derived from paper data), at up to 2.6x Frozen's compile time (55.2 s vs 21.1 s on 4,042 keys). Choose frozen (C++14, also has sets), mph (qlibs) or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash when you need a maintained GitHub project or an older compiler; only Frozen has been benchmarked head-to-head against static_maps.

**Gotchas:**
- operator[] does not check the key: an absent key either throws std::out_of_range (empty primary slot) or silently returns another key's value. Use at(), which compares the stored key, whenever input can fall outside the keyset. All published timings use the unchecked operator[].
- Builds are not reproducible by default: the RNG seed comes from __DATE__ and __TIME__, so each compile can pick different multipliers, table layout and compile time. The class constructors accept a seed_val argument, but the make_unordered_map factory does not expose one.
- Prefer make_unordered_map<data_array>() over the CTAD constructor: the constructor defaults to a 16-bit SIZE_T for up to 255 keys and does not check that truncated raw hashes are distinct. If two keys collide there, the secondary-multiplier search loops until the compiler's constexpr limit aborts the build.
- Only constexpr_hashes::hash<std::string_view> (DJB2), <int> and <std::size_t> (identity) exist, and the factory always uses hash<K>, so other key types need your own constexpr specialization. The header also does `using namespace constexpr_hashes;` at file scope and puts helpers such as seed() and RaggedArray in the global namespace, so its `hash` can clash with `using namespace std;`.

**Status:** Marked active, but the code is one figshare v1 deposit (2026-02-26) with no repo, issue tracker or later version; it is MIT-licensed and about a dozen small flat headers, so vendoring is the only integration path.

[repo](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31416038) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22506)

##### triehash  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Order-preserving minimal perfect hash generator emitting nested C switches for fixed string sets; 1.85-5x gperf's throughput in author's benchmark.

**Beats:** gperf — The numbers come from the author's 2016 hashbench. Each of 82 Debian Packages/Sources field names, plus 3 probe words, was looked up 1,000,000 times back-to-back in a static GCC -O2 build (GCC version not stated), against gperf generated with --pic --readonly-tables. On a Core i5-3320M, triehash reached 2.4 GB/s vs gperf's 1.3 case-sensitive (~1.85x) and 2.2 vs 0.7 case-insensitive (~3.1x). On Debian porterboxes of unstated CPU model, the case-sensitive gap reached ~5x (ppc64el, 2.0 vs 0.4) and the case-insensitive gap ~4x (arm64, 0.8 vs 0.2). re2c (1.7) and APT's unrolled AlphaHash (2.3) came close on the x230, and the repeated-word loop favors branchy switch code.

**How:** The keys go into a trie that is split by word length. The generated code is an outer `switch (length)` that dispatches to one function per length, and each of those is nested `switch` statements over 8-, 4- or 1-byte chunks read as unaligned integers on GNU C. The compiler turns these into compare/jump trees. There is no hash arithmetic, no data table and no final strcmp: reaching a leaf means every byte already matched, and a mismatch exits at the first differing chunk. In `--ignore-case` mode it ORs 0x20 into each chunk (e.g. `| 0x20202020`) wherever every key at that trie level is an unambiguous letter, so it needs no separate upper/lowercase cases. The author's blog reports about 4 instructions per byte.

**Use it when:**
- Small, fixed sets of field names, keywords or verbs known at build time (the benchmark used 82 Debian control-file field names) that you want mapped to an enum you then `switch` on.
- ASCII case-insensitive matching of such keys. This is where the gap to gperf is widest: 2.2 vs 0.7 GB/s on a Core i5-3320M, and 0.8 vs 0.2 on arm64.
- Tokenizers or parsers that already have (pointer, length). The function takes an explicit length, reads only bytes [0, length) and needs no NUL terminator.
- GCC/Clang builds on x86-64, ppc64el or arm64, where the multi-byte chunk reads are active and the reported speedups are largest.
- Plain C or mixed C/C++ codebases that want generated code with no runtime dependency beyond <stdint.h> and <stddef.h>.

**Skip it when:**
- Lookups on an unpredictable mix of keys. The benchmark hashed the same word 1,000,000 times in a row, so the branch predictor was fully trained on nested switches. Open issue #3 raises this and it was never re-measured with shuffled inputs.
- Large key sets (thousands of keys and up). Code size grows with the trie; the Debian package description itself says the generated code is 'larger' than gperf's, and there is no data beyond ~85 words.
- Key sets built at runtime, or lookups that must return a payload richer than an integer enum. gperf can return a user struct; with triehash you index your own array with the enum.
- MSVC or other non-GNU compilers, and ARM targets without unaligned access. These silently fall back to the byte-at-a-time switch, which was not benchmarked.
- Case-insensitive matching beyond ASCII. The 0x20 trick is ASCII-only.

**Integration:** source-drop · Perl at generation time (Debian package `triehash`); the generated code needs only <stddef.h> and <stdint.h> · Perl 5.14+ to run the generator: it uses package-block syntax, per issue #7, and CI covered Perl 5.14-5.28. Generated code is C with stdint.h. The multi-byte fast path needs GNU C (GCC/Clang: `__attribute__((aligned(1)))`, `__BYTE_ORDER__`); other compilers get the byte-wise fallback. It also builds as C++ via --enum-class (APT compiles it as .cc). · Any. Multi-byte reads work on GNU C little- and big-endian, are disabled automatically on ARM without __ARM_FEATURE_UNALIGNED, and can be forced off with TRIE_HASH_NO_MULTI_BYTE. Benchmarked on amd64, arm64, armel, armhf, ppc64el and mipsel.

**Vs siblings:** Pick triehash over ConstexprCore/perfect_hash or constexpr-phf (Kronuz), which also beat gperf but need C++ constexpr machinery, when you need plain C output or ASCII case-insensitive string-to-enum matching and can accept a Perl step at build time. In a C++17+ codebase that wants the compiler to build the table with no external generator, or needs mapped values rather than an enum, frozen or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash fit better; strager/perfect-hash-tables is research code rather than a packaged generator.

**Gotchas:**
- The POD documents `--namespace` and `--class` for C++, but GetOptions never registers them, so passing either aborts with 'Could not parse options!'. Only `--enum-class` and `--enum-name` (which accepts a qualified name such as `Foo::Bar`) work.
- Enum values follow input order. Inserting or removing a key mid-list renumbers every later value. APT's tagfile-keys.list warns that this order is part of libapt's ABI and should only be appended to.
- Non-members return `Unknown` with no hint, so callers need their own fallback path. APT falls back to a separate BetaHash bucket table for unknown fields.
- Multi-byte loads cast `&string[i]` to `uint64_t`/`uint32_t` typedefs with `aligned(1)` but no `may_alias`. They only work on GNU C, and 2-byte reads are off by default (`--multi-byte=320`) because the author found they slow older Intel CPUs. The README also cites GCC bug 77729, where the compiler inserts extra zero-extend instructions.

**Status:** Upstream has been abandoned since the last main commit on 2019-04-16 (Debian 0.3-3 was uploaded in 2020 and its packaging branch last touched in 2022). It is still a required build tool for APT and ships as 0.3-3 in every current Debian suite, and the MIT-licensed 728-line Perl script, or its generated C, is easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/julian-klode/triehash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/julian-klode/triehash#performance)

#### priority-queues-heaps

##### prio_queue (rollbear)  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Header-only B-heap priority queue storing priority/payload in separate arrays; faster than std::priority_queue on cache-friendly workloads.

**Beats:** std::priority_queue — On an Intel Core i7-4500U (Ubuntu 15.04, 32KB L1d, 64B cache lines) with g++ 4.9.3 -O3 -std=c++14 against libstdc++'s std::priority_queue, the author's blog graphs (no numeric text given) show the B-heap 'always faster' than std::priority_queue<int> across all tested mini-heap sizes (8/16/32/64), and 'consistently much faster' than std::priority_queue<pair<int,int>> when priority/payload are split into separate arrays, over 320 push+pop cycles at increasing queue sizes; the same post reports worse-or-comparable results for a std::pair<int, unique_ptr<msg>> payload.

**How:** Core technique is a B-heap layout (mini-heap size tunable as a power of two, e.g. 8/16/32/64) that groups a node's ancestors/descendants into the same cache line, cutting the cache misses a plain array-backed binary heap incurs on deep trees. It pairs this with a 'structure of arrays' split of priority and payload (a custom skip_vector) so comparisons during sift only touch the small, dense priority array and never pull large payload objects into cache. GCC builds additionally use __builtin_expect branch hints on the hot sift loops.

**Use it when:**
- Hot push/pop loops (event queues, schedulers, simulations) with small trivially-copyable priority keys (e.g. int) where std::priority_queue's array-of-struct layout causes cache misses
- Workloads where priority and payload can be stored/passed separately via push(key, value) rather than bundled into one pair/struct
- Throughput-oriented benchmarking over many push+pop cycles rather than a single latency-critical operation
- x86-64 GCC/Clang, C++14+ codebases willing to tune miniheap_size to the target cache line size (64 bytes in the reference hardware)
- Projects that want a dependency-free single header they can vendor without pulling in a build system

**Skip it when:**
- Payload is a large or non-trivial type such as std::pair<int, std::unique_ptr<msg>> — the author's own benchmark shows this configuration can be worse than or comparable to std::priority_queue
- You need a stable ordering among equal priorities — it's an unstable B-heap (confirmed by the maintainer in issue #2); add a discriminator field if insertion order matters
- You rely on container-adaptor features std::priority_queue doesn't even need to promise here but users may expect: iterators, merge, or swap are not implemented
- Concurrent/multi-threaded access — thread safety is not documented and there is no internal synchronization
- You need active maintenance: no CI/CMake in the repo, no open issues or PRs, last commit 2025-09-18, and the maintainer said in 2022 he'd probably just use std::vector<> if writing it today

**Integration:** header-only · none for the library itself (only <vector>, <cassert>, <tuple>, <cstddef>); self_test.cpp and perf_benchmark.cpp additionally pull in Catch2, trompeloeil, and the author's own tachymeter benchmarking header, but none of those are needed to use prio_queue.hpp · C++14 (uses std::enable_if_t); originally built and benchmarked with g++ 4.9.3 -O3 -std=c++14 · any (portable C++, no SIMD/intrinsics); __builtin_expect is used under __GNUC__ with a no-op fallback elsewhere; miniheap_size should be tuned to the target's cache line size (64 bytes assumed in the reference benchmarks)

**Vs siblings:** Pick prio_queue when priorities are not monotonically non-decreasing (not a Dijkstra-style access pattern), you need an arbitrary Compare rather than radix bucketing, and you want a tiny dependency-free C++ header. Prefer radix-heap/RadixHeap or S3Q when your workload fits their monotonic-priority or graph-search assumptions — they report larger, more concretely quantified speedups (radix-heap 1.2-1.7x, S3Q 4.6-7x) than this entry's graph-only, unstated ratios.

**Gotchas:**
- Not a stable sort: equal-priority elements are not ordered by insertion (maintainer confirmed in issue #2); add an insertion-sequence discriminator to Prio if you need stability
- miniheap_size must be a power of two and matched to the CPU cache line / Prio size for the claimed gains; size 8 was 'consistently bad' in the author's own tests
- The speedup depends on splitting priority and payload into separate push(key, value) calls; storing both in one struct/pair defeats the optimization and can be slower than std::priority_queue
- Exception guarantee is conditional: strong guarantee only if Prio and Value have noexcept move constructors/assignment; otherwise only the weak guarantee (per README)

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2025-09-18, no open issues or PRs, and no CI/CMake in the repo, but it's a single BSL-1.0 header small enough to vendor and re-benchmark yourself; the maintainer noted in a 2022 issue he'd likely design it differently (plain std::vector<>) today.

[repo](https://github.com/rollbear/prio_queue) · [benchmark](https://playfulprogramming.blogspot.com/2015/08/cache-optimizing-priority-queue.html)

##### radix-heap (pair_radix_heap)  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++ monotone radix heap: 1.2-1.7x faster than std::priority_queue on Dijkstra shortest-path workloads.

**Beats:** std::priority_queue — Benchmarked as pair_radix_heap vs. libstdc++'s std::priority_queue inside a standard Dijkstra implementation over DIMACS challenge-9 real USA road networks (264K to 24M vertices), compiled with gcc 4.6.3 -O3 on an Intel Xeon E5-2690 0 @ 2.90GHz / 256GB RAM / Linux 3.2.0, averaged over 100 random sources per graph. Pure priority-queue time was 1.40-1.74x faster (e.g. USA-road-t.USA.gr: 1.302186s vs 2.266316s); overall Dijkstra time including edge traversal was 1.12-1.29x faster (e.g. USA-road-t.USA.gr: 3.817832s vs 4.934690s), with the speedup shrinking on the smallest (264K-vertex NY) graphs.

**How:** Instead of a binary heap's comparison tree, it XOR-encodes keys into an order-preserving unsigned representation (internal::encoder, specialized for signed ints and IEEE float/double) and buckets each pushed key by the index of the highest bit where it differs from the last-extracted key (internal::find_bucket, via __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzll). Because extraction is monotone, popping only needs to redistribute the single lowest non-empty bucket into finer buckets one level at a time, rather than the O(log n) sift-down a binary heap performs on every pop -- giving O(1) amortized push and O(b) amortized pop where b is the key's bit width. This is the classic Ahuja/Mehlhorn/Orlin/Tarjan (1990) radix-heap algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Dijkstra's algorithm or other monotone-priority-queue algorithms over non-negative edge/cost weights
- Keys are native signed/unsigned integers or float/double (32- or 64-bit) that internal::encoder already handles
- Graph/grid search at the sizes benchmarked here (roughly 264K to 24M vertices), where the per-pop constant factor on the hot path matters
- Willing to vendor a single ~250-line header rather than pull in a build dependency
- Building with GCC or Clang (the bucket-index trick relies on their __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzll builtins)

**Skip it when:**
- Need a general-purpose priority queue where extracted keys can decrease (A*, event simulation with re-priority, negative edge weights) -- violates the monotonicity assert and corrupts the heap silently in release builds
- Need a custom comparator or non-numeric/composite keys -- there is no comparator template parameter, only the built-in integer/float encoders
- Need MSVC support out of the box -- code depends on GCC/Clang builtins, not verified against MSVC's intrinsics
- Need active maintenance -- no commits since 2015-05-16, single closed issue (a README-language request), CI last validated on gcc 4.8/clang 3.4
- Need in-place decrease-key/update or erase of a pushed element -- not exposed; only push, pop, and clear

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond the C++ standard library (<algorithm>, <array>, <cassert>, <climits>, <cstdint>, <limits>, <type_traits>, <utility>, <vector>) · C++11 (std::array, constexpr, variadic templates, std::piecewise_construct); CI-tested with gcc 4.8 and clang 3.4 per README/Travis badge · GCC/Clang (uses __builtin_clz/__builtin_clzll); not documented or tested on MSVC

**Vs siblings:** Pick radix-heap when the workload is specifically a monotone shortest-path search (Dijkstra-style, non-negative weights) over integer/float keys in C++ -- prio_queue (rollbear) and Superscalar Sample Queue (S3Q) are general-purpose std::priority_queue replacements without the monotonicity restriction and are the better choice when keys can decrease or aren't numeric. If the same monotone-Dijkstra pattern is needed in Rust, use radix_heap_rust instead, since this library has no Rust port.

**Gotchas:**
- push() enforces monotonicity only via assert(last_ <= x); in a release build compiled with NDEBUG a non-monotone push is silently accepted and produces wrong pop order rather than an error
- Each radix_heap/pair_radix_heap instance holds a fixed std::array of digits+1 std::vector buckets as members (33 buckets for 32-bit keys, 65 for 64-bit) -- more per-instance state than std::priority_queue's single vector, though the extra vectors are empty until pushes land in them
- No decrease-key, update, or erase of an already-pushed element -- only push/emplace, pop, top, clear
- Floating-point and signed-integer keys pass through an XOR bit-transform (internal::encoder) before bucketing; this is transparent through the public API but means the class is not usable with arbitrary user-defined key types, only the specializations provided

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit on 2015-05-16, but MIT-licensed (full license text in README.md, no separate LICENSE file) and a single ~250-line header, so it's cheap to vendor, read in full, and maintain yourself without upstream support.

[repo](https://github.com/iwiwi/radix-heap) · [benchmark](https://github.com/iwiwi/radix-heap/blob/master/example/README.md)

##### SimdQuickHeap  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

SIMD-accelerated Rust priority queue, ~12x faster than std::collections::BinaryHeap on large monotone-key workloads; i32/u32/i64/u64 only.

**Beats:** Rust std::collections::BinaryHeap — On an AMD EPYC 9684X (Zen4), Rust nightly release build (target-cpu=native, fat LTO, single codegen unit), the paper's Table 1 shows SimdQuickHeapAvx2 at 35.6 ns/elem and Avx512 at 32.2 ns/elem versus Rust std::collections::BinaryHeap at 439.6 ns/elem (~12.3x / ~13.7x) on a monotone-key push/pop workload at n=2^25; the gap shrinks to near-parity at n=2^10. No C++ std::priority_queue was benchmarked -- only Rust's BinaryHeap and several C++ competitors (Boost.Heap, S3Q, radix heap, original QuickHeap) via LLM-generated FFI wrappers.

**How:** Uses QuickSelect-style recursive partitioning of elements into buckets by pivot (median-of-3 by default), keeping only the bottom bucket sorted once it drops below a size threshold (N=16), so most of the heap stays partitioned rather than fully ordered. Partitioning and insertion use SIMD (AVX2, or AVX-512 when compiled in) to compare and move several keys per instruction. This avoids the pointer-chasing and cache misses of array/pointer-based binary heaps once the queue exceeds L2/L3 cache, matching the paper's finding that the gap over BinaryHeap is huge at n=2^25 and nearly gone at n=2^10.

**Use it when:**
- Priority queue over i32/u32/i64/u64 keys, large enough to exceed cache (paper's gains are at n=2^25; negligible at n=2^10)
- x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 available at compile time (target-cpu=native / -march=native)
- Monotone or near-sorted key sequences (Dijkstra-like, event queues, radix-heap-style workloads) -- where the paper's largest wins are shown
- Rust code that can pin to nightly (crate currently requires it) and can vendor a small, very new, unaudited crate
- C++ code able to build and statically/dynamically link a Rust cdylib and accept LLM-generated, unreviewed FFI bindings for a throughput win over a naive priority_queue

**Skip it when:**
- Keys can equal the type's MAX value (e.g. u64::MAX): open issue #6 shows pop() can silently return the wrong element because MAX is used internally as an empty-slot sentinel
- Need arbitrary Ord types, custom comparators, decrease-key, iteration, or merge -- only 4 fixed integer types and push/pop are supported
- No AVX2/AVX-512 target, or a stable-Rust-only build (crate needs nightly; issue #3 tracks moving off portable-simd)
- Heap stays small enough to fit in cache: measured advantage over BinaryHeap collapses to near-parity at n=2^10
- Need a mature, widely audited dependency: 35 stars, first public benchmark paper (ESA 2026, arXiv Sept 2026) with no independent replication, and an open correctness bug

**Integration:** crate · Rust: ensure_simd 0.1, rand 0.10, wide 1.2. C++ bindings: none beyond the compiled libquickheap.{so,dylib,a} plus quickheap.h/quickheap.hpp. · Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml pins channel = "nightly"); C++17 for the bindings example · x86-64 only; AVX2 or AVX-512 required at compile time. No other architectures documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over prio_queue (rollbear) or radix-heap when working in Rust against std::collections::BinaryHeap with one of the four supported integer key types and a large, cache-exceeding, monotone-ish workload; it is the only sibling using SIMD partitioning and the only one benchmarked directly against S3Q and monotone radix heaps (1.2-2.8x, more representative than the ~12x BinaryHeap figure). Prefer RadixHeap (radix_heap_rust) instead if you need stable-Rust maturity over a nightly-only crate with an open correctness bug.

**Gotchas:**
- Pushing the type's MAX value (e.g. u64::MAX) can corrupt later pop() results -- MAX is used as an internal empty-slot sentinel (issue #6, open, unresolved as of 2026-09-02)
- No LICENSE file in the repo (GitHub reports license: null); MIT is declared only via Cargo.toml's license field
- Requires nightly Rust today; issue #3 (open) tracks replacing portable-simd with the stable `wide` crate
- C++ bindings are explicitly LLM-generated and unreviewed; authors recommend building with panic="abort" so a Rust panic can't unwind across the FFI boundary

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-26) but very new (ESA 2026 paper, 35 stars) with an open, unresolved correctness bug on MAX-valued keys; usable as a copyable/vendorable crate, but MIT is only declared in Cargo.toml, not backed by a checked-in LICENSE file.

[repo](https://github.com/RagnarGrootKoerkamp/quickheap) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25681)

##### Superscalar Sample Queue (S3Q)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++17 cache-efficient priority queue beating std::priority_queue via batched, sample-sort-style bucket classification.

**Beats:** std::priority_queue — In a push+pop microbenchmark (2^13 to 2^27 elements) measured on GCC 9.3.0 -O3 (Ubuntu 20.04) across an Intel Xeon E5-2650 v2 and an AMD Athlon II X4 635, S3Q's speedup over min(S3QBH tuned binary heap, StdQueue) grows roughly logarithmically with N, reaching 4.6x-7x at the largest sizes; StdQueue in the benchmark harness is literally `std::priority_queue<T, std::vector<T>, std::greater<T>>` (confirmed in benchmarks/include/subjects/StdQueue.hpp), i.e. GCC's libstdc++ std::priority_queue.

**How:** It avoids per-insert branch mispredictions of a plain binary heap by batching pushes/pops and using a branchless, sample-sort-derived splitter classifier (borrowed from ips4o's classifier.hpp) to route items into buckets in bulk. Only a small base-case binary heap (sized to fit L1, `kBufBaseSize`, default ~32KiB/Item) is ever heap-ordered directly; the rest lives in coarser buckets that are split/merged in batches, giving amortized O(1/B log(M/B) N/M) cache misses per operation instead of O(log N) essentially-random accesses.

**Use it when:**
- Large queues (benchmark validated 2^13-2^27 elements) where cache-miss-driven throughput matters more than per-op latency
- Comparison-based key ordering needed with no monotonicity constraint (unlike radix heaps)
- Keys are mostly-unique or have modest duplication (see gotchas)
- C++17 project that can pull in ips4o, range-v3, and xoshiro as build dependencies
- Workload matches push/pop-heavy microbenchmark shape (bulk insert then repeated pop+push)

**Skip it when:**
- Workloads with many duplicate/near-duplicate keys: open issue #15 (opened 2026-04-10, still open) reports a stack overflow inserting millions of identical/near-identical keys; thesis 5.2.1 admits full duplicate-key handling is future work
- Need item keys at the extreme of the key's range (e.g. INT_MIN for i32 keys) — reserved internally as sentinels, confirmed problematic in issue #15
- Need a true drop-in for std::priority_queue's template interface (comparator + container) — S3Q requires a Cfg struct and different construction
- Concurrent/multi-threaded access — no synchronization in the code and thread safety is not documented
- Small queues that fit comfortably in L1 already — the bucket/classifier machinery adds setup overhead a plain heap doesn't need

**Integration:** header-only · ips4o (fork: raphinesse/ips4o, tag s3q.2), range-v3 (pinned commit 6f3d0e2af9ae), xoshiro (Reputeless/Xoshiro-cpp v1.1); benchmarks additionally pull tlx and raphinesse/SequenceHeap · C++17; thesis benchmarks used GCC 9.3.0 -O3. Closed issues #1, #5, #8 record and fix build failures on GCC 12-15 (-Werror=array-bounds, dangling-pointer warnings) · x86-64 tested in the thesis (Xeon E5-2650 v2, Athlon II X4 635); no SIMD intrinsics or arch-specific code visible in the headers I read, so likely portable, but only x86-64 is verified

**Vs siblings:** Pick S3Q over radix-heap/pair_radix_heap when keys aren't monotone or aren't well-suited to radix decomposition, since S3Q is purely comparison-based. Pick it over prio_queue (rollbear) when N is large enough (thesis tested up to 2^27) that cache-miss throughput dominates over a simpler binary-heap implementation; for smaller queues or simplicity, prio_queue's plain-heap approach avoids S3Q's extra dependencies and duplicate-key edge cases. If AVX2/AVX-512 hardware is available and the workload is monotone/constant-size, SimdQuickHeap is reported to beat S3Q itself by 1.4-2.8x.

**Gotchas:**
- Open issue #15 (still open as of 2026-05-27): stack overflow on inputs with large numbers of duplicate/near-duplicate keys; root cause is that overflowing buckets need enough distinct keys to split cleanly
- Item keys must avoid the extreme sentinel values of the key type (e.g. i32::MIN) — reserved internally for range bounds per the issue #15 discussion
- kBufBaseSize/kLogMaxDegree defaults are tuned for a 32KiB, 8-way, 64B-line L1D (per maintainer comment on issue #15); mismatched cache geometry may need retuning for best throughput
- Requires defining a Cfg struct per Item type (Item::key member or custom GetKey functor) — more upfront setup than a comparator-only API

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-05-27, three build/correctness issues closed in 2025, one duplicate-key stack-overflow issue still open); MIT-licensed and header-only so it's easy to vendor, but small (7 stars) and the duplicate-key edge case is unresolved.

[repo](https://github.com/raphinesse/s3q) · [benchmark](https://ae.iti.kit.edu/documents/theses/MA-von-der-Gr%c3%bcn.pdf)

#### random

##### cpp_batched_random  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only drop-in std::shuffle replacement that batches multiple Fisher-Yates draws from one 64-bit random word.

**Beats:** std::shuffle — Lemire's 2024-08-17 blog post shuffled std::vector<uint64_t> with std::mt19937_64, comparing std::shuffle to the predecessor batched_random::shuffle_2. On an Apple M2 (Apple/LLVM 15, libc++): 12.4 vs 2.4 ns/element at 10,000 elements and 12.0 vs 2.5 ns/element at 1,000,000 elements (~4.8-5.2x; author says 'four to five times faster'). On Linux with an unspecified Intel CPU (GCC 12, libstdc++): 2.2 vs 1.7 ns/element at 10,000 and 3.5 vs 2.7 ns/element at 1,000,000 (~1.3x; author says 'about 30% faster'). I re-fetched the blog page this session and confirmed these numbers match exactly.

**How:** Instead of drawing one bounded random value per swap like std::shuffle, it extracts up to 6 bounded Fisher-Yates indices from a single 64-bit random word using 128-bit multiply-shift (Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded-integer method, from Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, arXiv:2408.06213), amortizing each call to the underlying generator across multiple index draws. Batch size (2 through 6) is chosen based on how many elements remain, with rejection resampling on detected bias to keep the shuffle unbiased.

**Use it when:**
- Shuffling std::vector/array of trivially swappable elements with std::mt19937_64 (or any URBG with 64-bit output, min()==0, max()==UINT64_MAX).
- Running on libc++ (Apple/LLVM, e.g. macOS/iOS) where std::shuffle's bounded distribution is division-heavy -- biggest measured win (~4.8-5.2x).
- Throughput-sensitive shuffling (Monte Carlo simulations, dataset shuffling, deck/card simulations) where shuffle time is a measurable share of runtime.
- Header-only vendoring is acceptable -- single file, C++20 toolchain, no build-system integration beyond adding the header.
- Array size up to roughly 1 billion elements (technique requires the product of two ranges to fit in 64 bits, per the author).

**Skip it when:**
- RNG is 32-bit (std::mt19937, std::minstd_rand, etc.) -- fails to compile: static_assert requires result_type==uint64_t.
- Already on libstdc++/GCC -- measured gain shrinks to ~30%, may not justify the extra header dependency.
- Need a generic std::shuffle drop-in that works with arbitrary/non-standard URBGs without modification.
- Project is capped at C++17 or lacks 128-bit multiply support (no __uint128_t on GCC/Clang, no <__msvc_int128.hpp> on MSVC) -- CMakeLists.txt requires C++20.
- Tiny project (13 stars, zero issues filed) -- no track record of edge-case bug reports; read the ~120-line header yourself before trusting it in production.

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only: <iterator>, <concepts>, <type_traits>, <limits>; MSVC build also pulls <__msvc_int128.hpp>) · C++20 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20); needs __uint128_t (GCC/Clang) or MSVC's _Unsigned128 for 128-bit multiply · x86-64, aarch64 (anywhere __uint128_t or MSVC's __msvc_int128.hpp is available); CI covers Ubuntu and Windows (VS2022), blog benchmarks ran on Apple M2; no 32-bit platform support documented

**Vs siblings:** Siblings (PCG, Random123, wjakob/pcg32, xoshiro_cpp, biski64, AESRand, nanobench::Rng) replace the RNG itself; cpp_batched_random keeps whatever 64-bit URBG you already use (even std::mt19937_64) and instead speeds up the Fisher-Yates shuffle built on top of it. Pick this when you must keep std::mt19937_64 for reproducibility or statistical-quality reasons but still want faster shuffling, or stack it on top of a sibling 64-bit generator for compounding gains.

**Gotchas:**
- static_assert enforces result_type==uint64_t, min()==0, max()==UINT64_MAX at compile time -- passing std::mt19937 (32-bit) is a compile error, not a runtime one.
- Requires 128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t on GCC/Clang, std::_Unsigned128 via <__msvc_int128.hpp> on MSVC) -- a compiler/platform requirement beyond just C++20.
- The blog's headline numbers (4.8-5.2x on libc++, ~1.3x on libstdc++) were measured against batched_random::shuffle_2 in a 2024 prototype header, the direct predecessor of this repo; this repo's current batched_random::shuffle uses the same technique (multi-index batches from one 64-bit word) but was not itself the subject of those published numbers.
- The repo's own benchmarks/benchmark.cpp runs the identical std::shuffle vs batched_random::shuffle comparison but publishes no results in the repo -- you must build and run it yourself.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-02-28), dual MIT / Apache-2.0-with-LLVM-exception licensed, single ~120-line header with zero open issues and only 13 stars -- small enough to read in full and vendor directly.

[repo](https://github.com/lemire/cpp_batched_random) · [benchmark](https://lemire.me/blog/2024/08/17/faster-random-integer-generation-with-batching/)

##### PCG (pcg-cpp)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++11 PCG-family RNG beating std::mt19937/std::mt19937_64 raw-generation throughput by ~2.6-4x.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 / std::mt19937_64 — On zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks (Google Benchmark, pcg-cpp pinned at commit 428802d, clang -O3 -DNDEBUG, Intel Core i5-3570, no AVX2): pcg32_fast measured 1071.97M generations/s vs std::mt19937's 270.65M/s (~3.96x), and pcg64_fast measured 763.50M/s vs std::mt19937_64's 294.26M/s (~2.59x). Which C++ standard library (libstdc++ vs libc++) backed the std::mt19937 baseline is not stated in the benchmark.

**How:** Each engine keeps a small 64-bit or 128-bit linear/multiplicative congruential generator (LCG/MCG) state, permuted through an output function (XSH-RR, XSL-RR, XSH-RS) on every call, instead of Mersenne Twister's ~20,000-bit state array and tempering step -- so a generated value costs one multiply-add plus a permute rather than a big-array update. The benchmarked '_fast' variants are MCG-based (pcg32_fast = mcg_xsh_rs_64_32, pcg64_fast = mcg_xsl_rr_128_64): they drop the increment/stream-selection add that the default setseq/oneseq engines perform every step, shortening the instruction path at the cost of a single fixed stream per type.

**Use it when:**
- Raw uint32_t/uint64_t generation is the bottleneck (Monte Carlo inner loops, procedural generation, shuffling large arrays) and you don't need many independent streams.
- Code already consumes std::uniform_int_distribution or other <random> distributions -- PCG engines satisfy UniformRandomBitGenerator so distributions work unchanged.
- Non-cryptographic use where 64-bit (pcg32_fast) or 128-bit (pcg64_fast) internal state is acceptable.
- You can vendor a small, unmaintained header-only library (Apache-2.0/MIT dual-licensed) rather than depend on an actively-updated package.
- You want tunable stream separation later (setseq/oneseq/unique variants) without changing the surrounding API shape, if you outgrow the fast/MCG variant.

**Skip it when:**
- You need many statistically independent streams (e.g. one RNG per thread/worker) -- pcg32_fast/pcg64_fast are MCG-based with a single fixed stream; use the setseq variants (pcg32/pcg64) instead, at lower throughput.
- Cryptographic or security-sensitive randomness is needed -- PCG is not a CSPRNG and issue #27 ('Seed securely by default') is still open, so default seeding is not secure by default.
- Your code relies on seed()/set_stream() being independent -- issue #94 documents that calling seed() or seed(itype) on pcg32/pcg64 resets the stream to the default, silently discarding a previously-selected stream.
- You need an actively maintained upstream -- last commit 2022-04-08; issue #106 (Dec 2025) proposes a third-party fork (Total-Random/pcg-cpp) for Windows ARM64/MSVC/128-bit-fallback fixes that are unmerged upstream.
- You're touching custom seeding/streaming edge cases without testing -- several other open issues (#85, #91, #102) report surprising stream-selection/repeat behavior in specific variants; verify your exact typedef and seeding path.

**Integration:** header-only · none (pcg_random.hpp includes pcg_extras.hpp and pcg_uint128.hpp from the same repo, no external deps) · C++11 · any; uses __SIZEOF_INT128__/compiler builtins where available and has MSVC-specific intrinsic paths for 128-bit ops in pcg_uint128.hpp, but community issue #106 reports unmerged fixes needed for Windows ARM64 and some MSVC/128-bit-fallback cases

**Vs siblings:** Pick imneme/pcg-cpp over wjakob/pcg32 when you need 64-bit generation or explicit stream-separation strategies (oneseq/setseq/unique/mcg, extended k-dimensional generators) -- wjakob/pcg32 is a smaller single-header 32-bit-only PCG (940M gen/s, ~3.47x) with less machinery. Pick it over xoshiro_cpp when you want PCG's settable-stream model (C++11 SeedSequence support, per-stream selection) rather than xoshiro256++'s larger 256-bit-state, no-stream-argument design, even though xoshiro256++ measured similarly (946M gen/s, ~3.22x) on the same benchmark suite.

**Gotchas:**
- pcg32_fast/pcg64_fast are MCG-based (mcg_xsh_rs_64_32 / mcg_xsl_rr_128_64): one fixed stream per instance, no per-object stream selection.
- seed() and seed(itype) on pcg32/pcg64 reinstall the default stream, discarding any stream previously set via set_stream() (issue #94, open).
- No secure-by-default seeding -- issue #27 (open) asks for default construction to seed from OS entropy; currently you must seed explicitly.
- Repository is a reference implementation with many similarly-named typedefs (pcg32 vs pcg32_oneseq vs pcg32_fast vs pcg32_k64 ...); picking the wrong one changes both speed and stream-independence guarantees.

**Status:** Abandoned upstream -- last commit 2022-04-08, more than 3 years with no update; Apache-2.0/MIT dual-licensed and small enough to vendor as-is. A community fork (Total-Random/pcg-cpp, referenced in issue #106) exists for modern-platform fixes but is not merged upstream.

[repo](https://github.com/imneme/pcg-cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks)

##### wjakob/pcg32  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Tiny two-header PCG32 RNG beating std::mt19937 on speed, with an optional AVX2 8-wide variant.

**Beats:** std::mt19937 — In the zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks shootout (clang, -O3 -DNDEBUG, no -march flag, Intel i5-3570 @ 3.40GHz, 100 repetitions), pcg32::nextUInt averaged 940.39M gen/s vs std::mt19937's 270.65M gen/s (~3.47x). pcg32_8 measured 944.20M gen/s, but since this CPU has no AVX2, that number reflects the header's scalar 8-instance fallback path rather than the intended vectorized path.

**How:** Implements the PCG technique: a 64-bit linear congruential state advanced each step, with an XSH-RR permutation (xorshift on the high bits, then a data-dependent rotate) producing the 32-bit output. The 16-byte state and few-instruction step are cheaper than MT19937's 624-word state and tempering. pcg32_8 vectorizes eight independent PCG32 streams with AVX2 (32-bit lane multiplies via partial products, permutevar8x32 lane shuffles, variable-shift rotate) to emit 8 outputs per step on capable hardware.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk generation of 32-bit random values for non-cryptographic use (simulations, games, sampling)
- Need jump-ahead/jump-back (advance()) or stream-distance queries that std::mt19937 doesn't offer
- Want to vendor a tiny, dependency-free source drop (two headers) instead of linking a library
- Target CPU has AVX2 and the workload can batch draws 8 at a time (pcg32_8)
- MT19937-class statistical quality is sufficient; cryptographic security is not required

**Skip it when:**
- Cryptographic or adversarial contexts — neither PCG32 nor MT19937 is designed for that
- Need a native 64-bit output engine — this repo only has 32-bit pcg32 (use imneme/pcg-cpp for pcg64 variants)
- Code needs to satisfy std::uniform_random_bit_generator (e.g. pass the engine to std::uniform_int_distribution or std::shuffle) — pcg32 has no operator() or static min()/max()
- Building for a CPU without AVX2 while expecting the pcg32_8 speedup — it silently compiles to the scalar 8-instance fallback with no warning
- Need active upstream maintenance — no commits since June 2016 and an open 'Missing LICENSE' issue since 2021

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond the STL (pcg32.h: <inttypes.h>, <cmath>, <cassert>, <algorithm>; pcg32_8.h additionally: <immintrin.h>, <utility>, and includes pcg32.h) · not documented — no CMakeLists or pinned language standard; code uses only C++11-era features · pcg32.h: any platform with a C++ compiler; pcg32_8.h: x86-64 with AVX2 (guarded by #if defined(__AVX2__)), else compiles a portable scalar fallback

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over pcg-cpp (imneme/pcg-cpp) when you want the smallest possible PCG32-only source drop (two headers, no build system) rather than the full PCG engine family. On the same benchmark, pcg-cpp's pcg32_fast is about 14% faster (1071.97M vs 940.39M gen/s) and adds 64-bit engines, so prefer pcg-cpp when raw throughput or 64-bit output matters more than minimalism.

**Gotchas:**
- pcg32_8's AVX2 path is selected purely by the __AVX2__ macro at compile time; forgetting -mavx2 (or /arch:AVX2) silently yields the scalar fallback with no warning or error
- No operator()/min()/max(), so it can't be used as a standard UniformRandomBitGenerator with <random> distributions — use its own nextUInt(bound) or shuffle() instead
- Apache-2.0 is only stated in file header comments; there is no root LICENSE file, so GitHub reports 'no license' and an open issue (#2, 'Missing LICENSE', filed 2021) is still unresolved
- advance() and operator- assume both generators share the same inc (stream) value; this is only checked via assert(), which is compiled out in NDEBUG/release builds

**Status:** Abandoned since June 2016 (no further commits; an open 'Missing LICENSE' issue since 2021) but Apache-2.0-licensed (declared in file headers only) and small enough — two headers — to vendor as-is.

[repo](https://github.com/wjakob/pcg32) · [benchmark](https://github.com/zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks)

##### xoshiro_cpp (david-cortes)  `C++`  `CC0-1.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Header-only xoshiro256++/128++ wrapper that drop-in replaces std::mt19937(_64) for <random> distributions.

**Beats:** std::mt19937_64 — On zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks (Google Benchmark, 100 repetitions, clang -O3 -DNDEBUG, no architecture-specific flags, Intel i5-3570 @ 3.40GHz), xoshiro256++ generated 946.70M 64-bit values/s vs std::mt19937_64's 294.26M/s, about 3.2x, with both the benchmark source (src/xoshiro.cpp comparing directly against src/std.cpp) and the results table publicly readable.

**How:** Uses the xoshiro256++/128++ algorithm (Blackman & Vigna, 2019): a 256-bit (or 128-bit) state advanced with a few XORs, shifts and rotates per step, with a rotate-add-rotate output scrambler, no division and no large lookup tables, and a state small enough to sit in registers/L1 versus MT19937's ~2.5KB table and its tempering step. On the linked benchmark this measured 946.7M gen/s vs std::mt19937_64's 294.3M gen/s on the same hardware/compiler.

**Use it when:**
- Need higher raw 64-bit generation throughput than std::mt19937_64 for simulations, statistical/ML model initialization, or Monte Carlo work while keeping <random>-engine compatibility (distributions, std::shuffle)
- Want a much smaller generator state (32 bytes vs ~2.5KB for MT19937), e.g. per-thread or per-object RNG instances, or many concurrent generator states
- Need independent parallel streams: jump()/long_jump() advance the state by the canonical 2^128/2^192-draw offsets to split into non-overlapping subsequences (both methods and the correct jump-polynomial tables are present in xoshiro.h, confirmed by reading the source this session)
- Willing to vendor a single ~400-line public-domain header with no build step and no dependencies beyond the STL
- Non-cryptographic use where BigCrush-class statistical quality is enough

**Skip it when:**
- Need cryptographic-strength randomness: xoshiro256++ is explicitly not a CSPRNG
- Need output bit-for-bit reproducible with the reference prng.di.unimi.it implementation for a given integer seed: this wrapper's seed(uint64_t) path deliberately differs from the canonical seeding recipe (stated in the README)
- Rely on generator equality comparisons: operator== in both classes is implemented as a bare `return std::memcmp(...)` without comparing to 0, so it reports mismatched states as equal and identical states as unequal (verified by reading xoshiro.h this session) — do not use it
- Need an actively maintained or widely-adopted dependency: single-star, single-file personal project, no commits since 2021-09-08, no LICENSE file (CC0 notice only in source/README)
- Need runtime-selectable, arbitrary-count independent streams the way PCG offers (per-instance odd increment); xoshiro here only offers the two fixed jump offsets

**Integration:** header-only · none (STL only: <iostream>, <cstring>, <cstdint>) · C++11 (per README); code compiles conditionally for C++20 to drop the explicit operator!= · any — portable C++ using bit rotations and memcpy, no SIMD or architecture-specific intrinsics; benchmark itself ran on x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over PCG (pcg-cpp / wjakob pcg32) when you specifically want the xoshiro256++ statistical profile with built-in jump()/long_jump() streams in one dependency-free header; on the same benchmark PCG's pcg64_fast is slower (763.5M/s) while pcg32_fast is faster but 32-bit only (1072M/s). If raw throughput matters more than the specific algorithm, AESRand (27-34 GB/s, requires AES-NI) or biski64 (~2.5x std::mt19937_64) beat xoshiro256++ by a wide margin on their own benchmarks.

**Gotchas:**
- operator== is `return std::memcmp(...)` without `== 0`, so it evaluates backwards (identical states compare unequal, differing states compare equal) — confirmed in xoshiro.h this session; don't use it for equality checks
- Default-constructed instances start from a fixed hardcoded state (not randomly seeded), the same gotcha as std::mt19937's default constructor — call seed() explicitly for non-deterministic output
- Seeding logic is intentionally different from the canonical prng.di.unimi.it recipe (README: 'small change in the seeding logic'), so output won't match the reference C implementation for the same integer seed
- No LICENSE file in the repo, only a CC0 dedication noted in the README and the source header comment — a compliance process that requires an actual LICENSE file will flag this

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit on 2021-09-08 (1 star, 1 fork, 0 open issues, no PRs) but it's a single ~400-line CC0/public-domain header with no LICENSE file — trivial to vendor and audit, so the lack of maintenance is low-risk beyond the license-file gap.

[repo](https://github.com/david-cortes/xoshiro_cpp) · [benchmark](https://github.com/zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks)

##### Random123  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Header-only counter-based CPU/GPU RNG family (Philox, Threefry, ARS); only AES-NI variants clearly beat std::mt19937_64.

**Beats:** std::mt19937_64 — In the peer-reviewed SC11 paper's Table 2 (confirmed directly from the PDF), on a 3.07GHz quad-core Xeon X5667 (Westmere) with gcc 4.5.3 and no stated optimization flags, std::mt19937_64 (the C++0x/libstdc++ engine) ran at 6.1 GB/s; the AES-NI-accelerated ARS-7 reached 11.1 GB/s (~1.8x) and ARS-5 reached 17.8 GB/s (~2.9x), while the portable, no-special-hardware Threefry-4x64-20 reached 6.4 GB/s, only a marginal ~1.05x.

**How:** Because each call is a pure function of (counter, key) with no state to read-modify-write, the generators vectorize and parallelize trivially and avoid the roughly 2.5KB of per-thread state std::mt19937 needs. ARS and AESNI reuse the hardware AES-NI round function directly, so on supporting CPUs ARS-7 needs only about 1.1 cycles/byte (ARS-5 about 0.7). Threefry (ARX rounds derived from the Skein/Threefish hash) and Philox (Feistel network plus one wide integer multiply per round) get most of their speed from a handful of cheap integer ops per output word rather than a large state-shuffle step.

**Use it when:**
- Monte Carlo / stochastic simulation workloads needing millions of independent, reproducible streams addressed by (counter,key) instead of stored per-thread generator state
- CUDA/OpenCL/Metal GPU kernels or heavily multithreaded CPU code, where per-thread state size and synchronization matter more than single-core throughput
- x86 CPUs with AES-NI, where ARS-7/ARS-5 give a real ~1.8x-2.9x throughput win over std::mt19937_64 (11.1-17.8 GB/s vs 6.1 GB/s)
