- UnmarshalVT on a non-zeroed message behaves like proto.Merge rather than a fresh Unmarshal; call Reset() first or use a freshly allocated message.
- Memory pooling is opt-in per message (`option (vtproto.mempool)` or `--go-vtproto_opt=pool=...`) and, as of issue #162, only pools the outer message — nested/child messages are still freshly allocated on each unmarshal.
- Returning a pooled repeated-field message has open correctness bugs (issue #92, generated ResetVT); verify pool behavior with your own message shapes before relying on it in production.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-02, 1118 stars, used in production by Vitess/PlanetScale and widely adopted in the Go gRPC ecosystem); BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but 'copyable' here means installing the plugin and wiring it into your protoc invocation, not literally copying a header.

[repo](https://github.com/planetscale/vtprotobuf) · [benchmark](https://vitess.io/blog/2021-06-03-a-new-protobuf-generator-for-go/)

##### Zserio  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Own-IDL C++/Java/Python serialization framework; bit-packed decode 1.2x-2.6x faster than protoc.

**Beats:** protoc — Per-decode time (protobuf ParseFromString vs zserio read, pre-serialized blob, JSON load/serialize untimed) on 4 schemas, gcc 11.3.0 CMake-Release build, Intel i7-9850H/Linux Mint 21.1: Zserio beat protoc-generated C++ by 1.17x-2.63x (addressbook 1.478 vs 1.731ms, apollo 0.244 vs 0.641ms, carsales 1.374 vs 2.053ms, simpletrace 0.221 vs 0.386ms); byte-aligned variants reached 2.05x and 2.22x. Benchmark is first-party (same org as Zserio, 6-star companion repo), evidence tier C.

**How:** Zserio packs fields at the bit level rather than byte level, and its default schemas carry no per-field tag IDs or explicit length prefixes the way protobuf's wire format does, so there is less to scan per field during decode. Byte-aligning fields (the '_align' schema variants) trades blob size for speed by removing bit-shift work, cutting decode time roughly another 40-45% versus the default schema on addressbook and carsales in this benchmark. No SIMD or algorithmic trick is documented; the win is wire-format layout, not a decode algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Designing a new wire format from scratch where blob size matters as much as decode speed
- Multi-language C++/Java/Python project willing to author .zs schemas instead of .proto
- Need built-in SQLite table serialization, JSON debug export, or generic reflection/services without hand-rolling them
- Functional-safety-conscious C++ codebase: C++11 runtime, >600 unit tests, ASan/UBSan clean, 99% line coverage
- Deserialize-heavy workloads (parse once, read many) where a 1.2x-2.6x per-decode win compounds

**Skip it when:**
- Already invested in protobuf schemas, tooling, or cross-org interop; migration cost likely exceeds the modest measured speedup
- Need protobuf-style forward/backward field compatibility; Zserio's compactness comes partly from dropping field IDs and lengths
- Team can't add a Java-based external compiler step (zserio.jar) to the build
- Need platforms beyond 64/32-bit Linux and 64-bit Windows; macOS/ARM are not in the stated Supported Platforms list
- Want a larger, independently verified speedup: siblings RapidProto (~7x) and vtprotobuf (~1.7x) show bigger measured wins over protoc

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the C++ runtime itself; bundled SQLite3 only if using the SQL-database extension; Java (JRE) needed at build time to run the zserio.jar code generator, not at runtime · C++11; gcc 7.5.0+ (11.4.0/7.5.0 tested), clang 11.0.0+ (14.0.6/21.1.8 tested), MinGW 7.5.0+, MSVC 2017+; CMake 3.15+ if using the bundled CMake helper · 64-bit Linux, 32-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows per README's Supported Platforms list; macOS/ARM not stated

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zserio when you want a full schema framework (SQLite mapping, JSON debug strings, services/pub-sub, one schema for C++/Java/Python) and can move off .proto. Pick RapidProto or vtprotobuf instead if you must keep .proto files and want a bigger measured decode speedup with less schema-language lock-in.

**Gotchas:**
- Byte-aligned (_align) and delta-packed (_packed) schema variants trade blob size against decode speed in opposite directions; pick per workload
- Compact wire format omits field tags/lengths, so schema-evolution/compatibility rules differ sharply from protobuf's
- Code generated by the zserio compiler inherits the license of the input .zs schema, separate from the BSD-3-Clause runtime license
- Open issue #577 'Consider to optimize C++ serialization performance' (still open) indicates maintainers see further headroom

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-17, frequent releases); BSD-3-Clause runtime, with generated code separately licensed under the input schema's license.

[repo](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio-protobuf-benchmarks)

## Copyleft

### numerics-and-science

#### blas-lapack

##### Eigen  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++ template library for dense/sparse linear algebra; beats OpenBLAS at small-to-mid sizes without linking BLAS.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS — On an Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y (GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, single-threaded), Eigen's own kernels beat OpenBLAS 0.3.26's geometric-mean GFLOP/s on GEMV, DOT, TRSM, POTRF and SYEV across most size bands (roughly 1.1-4.9x), are near parity on large GEMM, and lose on GEEV and GESDD; against Intel oneMKL 2025.3, Eigen is generally slower at large sizes. The harness (Google Benchmark 1.8.3, median of 10 reps) is public but still an unmerged GitLab merge request (!2903), and frequency was not locked during the run.

**Independent measurement:** Eigen 5.0.1 reached 193.1 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (91% of the host's measured single-core FMA peak of 212.2, 1.42x a hand-written xsimd kernel, 1.85x Blaze), but lost fixed 4x4 multiplies to a naive triple loop (5.87 vs 3.20 ns, naive 1.83x) and 3x3 to hand-rolled xsimd (5.59 vs 2.26 ns, 2.5x). At N=64 hand-rolled xsimd also beat it 1.41x (187.4 vs 133.2 GFLOP/s), and the naive 4x4 win is gcc-specific (clang 18 leaves that loop scalar and Eigen wins there). (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13 -O3 -march=native, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**Independent measurement:** Built without -march=native, Eigen fell from 193.1 to 34.6 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (5.6x loss), while OpenBLAS with runtime CPU dispatch went from 575.9 to 569.2. sizeof(struct{Eigen::Matrix4f; char;}) is 80/96/128 bytes under SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512, so translation units built with different arch flags silently disagree on layout. (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**How:** Expression templates fuse chained operations into a single loop at compile time, avoiding temporaries. Eigen's own GEMM kernel does three-level cache blocking -- mc x kc panels packed for L2/L3, mr x kc micro-panels kept in L1, and a register-blocked micro-kernel -- the same family of technique GotoBLAS/BLIS use, confirmed in the header comment of GeneralBlockPanelKernel.h. Kernels are explicitly SIMD-vectorized (SSE/AVX/AVX-512/NEON/etc.), and small fixed-size matrices get compile-time loop unrolling that skips packing overhead entirely, which is why Eigen's edge over OpenBLAS is largest at small sizes (DOT 4.9x, GEMV 2.2x at n<=16) and shrinks or reverses as size grows.

**Use it when:**
- Small and medium dense ops (roughly n<=1024) where OpenBLAS's dispatch/call overhead dominates -- GEMV and DOT measured 1.1-4.9x faster than OpenBLAS here
- You want a header-only dependency with no external BLAS/LAPACK to build, package, or version-pin
- Fixed-size or compile-time-sized linear algebra (small transforms, small solvers) where Eigen's unrolled kernels apply
- TRSM, POTRF, SYEV workloads at small/mid size, where Eigen beat OpenBLAS by 1.25-3.6x per this benchmark
- C++ codebases that want expression-template ergonomics instead of raw BLAS call signatures

**Skip it when:**
- Very large dense GEMM/SYRK (n in the 1500+ range) where Eigen is roughly at parity with OpenBLAS and often slower than oneMKL
- GEEV (nonsymmetric eigenvalues) -- measured at 0.45x OpenBLAS at 192-1024, and well behind oneMKL at large sizes
- GESDD (SVD) at mid-to-large sizes -- measured 0.6-0.9x OpenBLAS
- Large-scale multi-threaded numerics -- this benchmark and Eigen's own kernels are single-threaded; OpenMP only parallelizes some ops (dense GEMM, PartialPivLU, a few iterative sparse solvers), not the full LAPACK surface
- Storing fixed-size Eigen objects in STL containers or passing them by value without alignment care -- triggers runtime alignment assertions on SIMD builds

**Integration:** header-only · none (STL only); optional external BLAS/LAPACK backend for large-matrix offload · C++14 (target_compile_features cxx_std_14 in CMakeLists.txt); CMake 3.18+ only needed for the optional install/test build, not for using the headers · x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 optional), aarch64/ARM NEON, PowerPC Altivec/VSX, MIPS MSA; this benchmark ran on AVX-512

**Vs siblings:** no siblings catalogued yet

**Gotchas:**
- Fixed-size vectorizable types (Vector4d, Matrix4d, Quaternionf, etc.) assert at runtime if misaligned -- avoid storing them by value in STL containers or passing by value without EIGEN_MAKE_ALIGNED_OPERATOR_NEW
- OpenMP thread count should match physical cores, not logical/hyperthreads -- oversubscription slows things down since Eigen's kernels already saturate a core
- Heavy expression-template usage increases compile times
- For very large dense problems, Eigen's own docs and this benchmark both point toward linking an external BLAS/LAPACK backend instead of relying solely on Eigen's kernels

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23) with a large downstream user base (ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, OpenCV, Blender); MPL-2.0, header-only, trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen) · [benchmark](https://libeigen.gitlab.io/benchmarks/2026-09-xeon-gold-6444y-blas-lapack-avx512/)

### parsing-and-text

#### parser-generators-and-combinators

##### PAPAGENO (PArallel PArser GENeratOr)  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Bison-style generator that emits pthreads-parallel operator-precedence parsers, up to 5.5x faster than Flex+Bison on ARM.

**Beats:** GNU Bison + GNU Flex (sequential LALR(1) parser/lexer) — The paper (Barenghi et al., preprint for Science of Computer Programming) benchmarks the PAPAGENO-generated parallel lexer/parser against the authors' own sequential Flex+Bison LALR(1) reference parser, both built with gcc 4.9.1 -O3 -march=native, on a 16-core quad-Opteron 8378 server and a 4x-Cortex-A15 Odroid-XU ARM board, over real-world JSON (2.7KiB-75MiB) and Lua (7KiB-35MiB) inputs. It reports up to 5.5x speedup on the ARM board and a separate maximum 7x speedup for parallel lexing alone vs. sequential Flex (not vs. the full Flex+Bison pipeline); the 16-core server JSON comparison (Fig. 13b) is a 3D plot with no stated exact peak number against Flex+Bison.

**How:** Exploits the OPG property that the shift/reduce decision between two adjacent terminals depends only on a fixed precedence relation, not on global parse state, so the input can be split into chunks and reduced independently on separate POSIX threads with no wasted re-computation when recombining partial trees. Lexing can likewise be split into an independent parallel pass (test/JSON_parallel_lexer). The README states throughput scales close to linearly with thread count on JSON workloads.

**Use it when:**
- Files large enough for parallelism to amortize thread overhead (paper shows real gains mainly on multi-MB inputs, up to 75MiB JSON / 35MiB Lua)
- A grammar that is already an Operator Precedence Grammar, or small enough to convert without exploding the rule set (e.g. arithmetic expressions, JSON)
- Batch/offline C parsing on multi-core x86_64 servers or ARM big.LITTLE boards where lexing/parsing is a proven bottleneck
- You can vendor and maintain generated C source yourself (Python 2.x generator, no upstream releases since 2015)

**Skip it when:**
- General LALR(1) or ambiguous/context-free grammars: converting real-world Lua to OPG+Fischer-normal-form blew productions up from 144 to 8547 plus required manual lexer transforms
- Small or streaming inputs (KB-scale) — paper reports negligible or negative speedup there from thread migration/NUMA overhead
- Anywhere you need Bison's GLR mode or ANTLR-style handling of ambiguous grammars — OPG is a strict LALR(1) subset
- Projects needing an actively maintained tool or Python 3 support: last commit 2015-04-20, generator is Python 2.x only, one unresolved GitHub issue
- Anywhere a true drop-in Bison/Flex replacement is required — grammar syntax is Bison-like but the generated parser's call signature and build process differ

**Integration:** source-drop · Python 2.x to run the generator; GNU Flex, gcc/clang, Make, and POSIX threads (pthreads) to build the generated parser · Python 2.x (generator); C with pthreads and GNU Flex for the generated code (paper's own build used gcc 4.9.1, -O3 -march=native) · x86_64 and ARM (tested on Cortex-A15/A7); requires a POSIX threads implementation (tested on Linux NPTL)

**Vs siblings:** Pick PAPAGENO only when the win you need is multi-core parallelism on a Bison-compatible C grammar that is (or can be forced into) Operator Precedence form; the catalogued siblings (flap, re2c, Pika Parser, winnow, chumsky, MPL/FastParse) are all single-threaded OCaml/Rust tools that get their speedups from fused lexing, code generation, or SIMD/table specialization, not from splitting work across cores, so they don't compete on this axis.

**Gotchas:**
- Generator statically rejects non-OPG grammars (consecutive nonterminals, precedence conflicts) and only prints diagnostics — you must manually restructure the grammar
- Real-world grammars can blow up drastically under OPG conversion: Lua went from 144 to 8547 productions in the paper's benchmark
- README states terminal/nonterminal names may not start with '_'
- Generator itself is Python 2.x only; no indication of a Python 3 port

**Status:** Abandoned: no commits since 2015-04-20, GPL-2.0 licensed, one open GitHub issue and no CI/releases; small enough (a handful of C files plus a Python 2.x code generator) to vendor and maintain yourself if you accept the OPG grammar restriction.

[repo](https://github.com/PAPAGENO-devels/papageno) · [benchmark](https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/handle/11311/971391/67830/papaj-final.pdf)

### serialization-and-formats

#### yaml-toml-xml

##### Parshred  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++20 SIMD XML parser with a flat 32-byte-node DOM; 1.6-3.3x pugixml's read-only parse throughput on synthetic XML.

**Beats:** pugixml — Setup: generated <item id name status>text</item> records at 64 KB-128 MB, single thread, Ryzen 5 7640U, GCC 16.1 -O3 -mavx2. fast_dom_parse<FDOM_FASTEST>, which builds no text nodes, ran at 1317-2722 MB/s against pugixml 1.14 load_buffer(parse_minimal) at 641-1585 MB/s, a 1.6x-3.3x gap. It matched RapidXML 1.13 parse_fastest within ~5% up to 16 MB and was 1.5-1.8x faster at 64-128 MB. These are first-party numbers, and pugixml copies the buffer and still builds PCDATA nodes, so the pugixml ratio overstates a same-work comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Its fast DOM parsers do not validate: end-tag mismatches are not reported (the project's own W3C run accepts 928 of 1,383 not-well-formed cases), fast_dom_parse drops CDATA and leaves entities undecoded unless FDOM_NORMALIZE is passed, values over 65,535 bytes are truncated, and deep nesting silently produces a wrong tree. The SIMD path needs the caller built with -mavx2.

**How:** It makes a single pass over the input. AVX2 32-byte compare+movemask+ctz scans (_mm256_cmpeq_epi8/_mm256_movemask_epi8) jump to the next '<', closing quote or comment/CDATA end, and names are read with a scalar lookup table. Nodes are 32-byte structs written in order into one malloc'd array, which starts at len/35 nodes and doubles with realloc. They are linked by uint32 indices, not pointers, and names and attribute values stay as pointers or offsets into the input (zero-copy). The benchmarked FDOM_FASTEST mode also skips building text nodes. The parser never matches end-tag names or reports errors, so it does less work than pugixml. The author puts the 64 MB+ gap over RapidXML down to RapidXML's per-node allocation versus this one flat array.

**Use it when:**
- Read-only extraction of element structure and attributes (not text) from trusted, well-formed UTF-8 XML, which is exactly the FDOM_FASTEST shape that was benchmarked
- Large documents (64-128 MB) on x86-64 with AVX2, where the README shows 1.5-1.8x over RapidXML and 1.85-2.6x over pugixml
- Replacing a pugixml load_buffer + walk used only for reading, when you can adopt an index-based API with string_view results and keep the input buffer alive
- Python batch jobs over trusted XML that need more than lxml's roughly 90-106 MB/s (README reports 527-575 MB/s), provided raw, entity-undecoded text is acceptable
- Open-source projects already under AGPL-3.0-or-later, or teams willing to buy the commercial license

**Skip it when:**
- Untrusted or possibly malformed input: neither fast_dom_parse nor dom_parse checks that end tags match or reports parse errors. The project's own W3C run shows 928 of 1383 not-wf cases wrongly accepted (SAX path)
- Closed-source products or SaaS without a paid license: AGPL-3.0 §13 network-use copyleft, whereas pugixml (MIT) and RapidXML are permissive
- Files of 64 KB-16 MB where you already use RapidXML: Parshred's own table shows parity within ~5% there, and RapidXML is header-only
- Needs beyond read-only DOM: editing the tree in place, pugixml's full XPath 1.0 (ancestor/preceding axes and variables are missing), namespace-aware DOM/XPath, or UTF-16/Latin-1 input (UTF-8 only)
- Workloads that need production maturity: single author, 0 stars, and all code landed 2026-07-11 to 07-29 with no commits since. The weekly fuzz job has failed twice in fuzz_xpath (out-of-memory in xpath::eval_step and UBSan float-to-integer overflow in xpath.hpp)

**Integration:** static lib · none at runtime (vcpkg.json lists none); GoogleTest and Google Benchmark are fetched only for tests/benchmarks; pybind11 only for the Python module · C++20; README: GCC 12+, Clang 15+, MSVC 2022+; CMake 3.20+ (CI builds GCC 13, Clang 17, AppleClang on macos-14, MSVC 2022) · x86-64 (README says SSE4.2 minimum, but FastDOM's SIMD needs your own TU compiled with -mavx2) and aarch64 (NEON helpers exist but are not called by the FastDOM/SAX paths checked, so scalar there); Linux, macOS, Windows

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over RapidXml when documents are 64 MB or larger (1.5-1.8x in its own table) or when you want XPath and Python bindings, and AGPL or a commercial license is acceptable; below 16 MB, RapidXml is at parity, header-only and permissively licensed. Against libsimdxml (about 1.2-1.25x over pugixml on an old i7) it claims a bigger pugixml margin, but on different hardware and a synthetic workload. Use SpeedyXml instead for measured real-world streaming.

**Gotchas:**
- The parsers lose data silently. fast_dom_parse drops CDATA sections entirely and leaves entities undecoded unless you pass FDOM_NORMALIZE. value_len is a uint16, so values over 65535 bytes are truncated. Nesting beyond 255 levels (64 for dom_parse) quietly corrupts the tree, even though conformance.md claims dom_parse throws at depth 512. The Python binding uses fast_dom_parse<0>, so Python users hit the CDATA and entity behaviour too.
- fast_dom_parse chooses SIMD at compile time: simd_utils.hpp is gated on #ifdef __AVX2__, so a TU built without -mavx2/-march gets scalar byte loops. The CPUID runtime dispatch covers only the simd_scan backends, and the PyPI binding module is built with plain -O3.
- FastDom stores raw pointers and 32-bit offsets into the caller's buffer, so the buffer must outlive the DOM. Offsets and indices are uint32, which implies a 4 GiB input limit (not documented). Parent lookup (XPath '..') scans the whole node array, O(n).
- parallel_fast_dom_parse splits only where nesting depth returns to 0, so a normal single-root document falls back to serial. The README's FetchContent snippet pins v0.1.0, but the latest tag is v0.1.6. Some docs are stale: performance.md has older numbers, and the migration guide describes an 80-byte XmlNode with a parent pointer, but the code has a 64-byte node with no parent.

**Status:** Young single-author project (created 2026-07-11, last commit 2026-07-29 at v0.1.6, also on PyPI, 0 stars, no issues filed). It is usable under AGPL-3.0-or-later or a paid commercial license, not permissively.

[repo](https://github.com/gregghy/parshred) · [benchmark](https://github.com/gregghy/parshred#c-dom-throughput-x86-64-avx2)

### stdlib-replacements

#### async-tasks-threadpools

##### libfork  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++20/23 coroutine fork-join library beating oneTBB and OpenMP on fine-grained task throughput and memory.

**Beats:** oneTBB (Intel Threading Building Blocks) and OpenMP (libomp) — The arXiv:2402.18480 preprint (Williams & Elliott) benchmarked libfork 3.5.0 against oneTBB 2021.10.0, Clang-bundled OpenMP/libomp, and Taskflow 3.6.0 on fib(42), integration, matmul, nqueens(14), and UTS tree-search, compiled with Clang 18.0.0 at the paper's 'highest optimization setting,' on 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (112 cores, 2 NUMA nodes, 500GiB RAM), swept from 1-112 cores. Abstract-stated averages are 2.7x faster / 6.2x less memory than oneTBB and 7.2x faster / 10x less memory than OpenMP; the frequently quoted 7.5x/19x (vs TBB) and 24x/24x (vs OpenMP) figures are peak ratios on the fib benchmark specifically at 112 cores, not typical-case numbers.

**How:** A continuation-stealing work-stealing scheduler lets the worker that forks a task keep running the child immediately while only the continuation is exposed to be stolen, minimizing deque traffic on the common path. Coroutine frames are placed on an (almost) non-allocating 'cactus stack' built from segmented stacks instead of being heap-allocated per task, giving fork/call overhead about 10x a bare function call. NUMA-aware pools (optionally using hwloc for topology detection) reduce cross-socket stealing cost, which the paper credits for near-linear time and memory scaling up to 112 cores.

**Use it when:**
- Very fine-grained recursive divide-and-conquer workloads (fib-style, tree search, numerical integration) where oneTBB/OpenMP per-task overhead dominates runtime
- Codebases willing to rewrite hot-path functions as C++20 coroutines (lf::task<T>) rather than keep existing std::async/TBB/OpenMP call sites unchanged
- Multi-socket/NUMA machines with high core counts (paper benchmarked 1-112 cores, 2 NUMA nodes) where linear time/memory scaling matters
- Workloads where peak RSS is as important as speed - libfork's memory footprint was measured far below TBB/OpenMP/Taskflow on the UTS tree-search benchmark
- Projects that can pin a recent compiler (current main requires C++23 per CMakeLists) via CMake, vcpkg, or Conan

**Skip it when:**
- Any deployment target still on MSVC: BUILDING.md states libfork compiles on MSVC 19.35-19.37 but seg-faults at runtime due to an open Visual Studio symmetric-transfer/coroutine codegen bug
- Coarser-grained parallel loops: a real integration into BLIS's GEMM (issue #113) showed libfork's busy_pool at only 55% of OpenMP's GFLOPS at matrix dim=512, only beating OpenMP once dim >= 2048, partly because libfork lacks a flat bulk-spawn/parallel_invoke API
- Teams unwilling to convert call sites to coroutine-returning lf::task<T> and to handle its exception_before_join + rethrow-on-join exception model
- Older/unpatched compilers: Clang <=16 needs a thread_local workaround with a performance penalty, and GCC below -O2 can stack-overflow because it doesn't guarantee coroutine symmetric-transfer tail calls
- Anyone requiring peer-reviewed evidence: the only performance writeup is an arXiv v1 preprint (Feb 2024) with no journal/conference publication, and its headline 'up to' ratios are peak fib/integrate figures at 112 cores, well above the abstract's stated averages (2.7x/7.2x)

**Integration:** header-only · none required beyond a compiler and Threads; optional hwloc >=2.5.0 for NUMA topology detection (LF_USE_HWLOC) · C++20 per docs (C++23 preferred); current main CMakeLists.txt sets target_compile_features(... cxx_std_23) on the library interface target. Compiler support table: Clang 15-18 (16 and below need a thread_local workaround with a perf penalty due to LLVM bugs #63022/#47179), GCC 11-13 (needs >= -O2 for guaranteed coroutine tail calls), Apple Clang (Xcode-shipped, with the same old-Clang mitigations), MSVC 19.35-19.37 compiles but seg-faults at runtime · Linux, macOS, Windows CI configured (linux.yml/macos.yml/windows.yml), any arch with a conforming C++20/23 coroutine compiler; NUMA-aware scheduling is opt-in via hwloc

**Vs siblings:** Pick libfork over TooManyCooks/dispenso/Taskflow when the workload is extremely fine-grained recursive fork-join (fib-like or UTS-style tree search) run across dozens to 100+ cores and peak memory matters as much as latency; TMC and dispenso report comparable 'beats oneTBB' wins with a simpler non-coroutine API and less compiler sensitivity, so prefer them if you don't want to rewrite call sites as C++20/23 coroutines or can't guarantee a modern compiler.

**Gotchas:**
- Strict fork-join is enforced: every forked/called child must be joined with co_await lf::join before the parent task returns - there is no fire-and-forget
- Exceptions from a child surfaced before the join point arrive as exception_before_join; you must catch it and still call join, which then rethrows the child's real exception (include/libfork/core/exceptions.hpp)
- Current main branch requires C++23 (cxx_std_23 in CMakeLists.txt) even though the README/BUILDING.md prose still advertises 'C++20 coroutines' - check your compiler before adopting HEAD
- MSVC builds compile but crash at runtime (known upstream MSVC coroutine codegen bug); do not ship an MSVC build without testing

**Status:** Actively maintained - default-branch last commit 2026-01-17 - and header-only/copyable under MPL-2.0, so it can be vendored without a package manager, but current HEAD needs a C++23-capable compiler, MSVC support is presently broken at runtime, and the last tagged release (v3.8.0) is from 2024-05-10 with substantial unreleased work since.

[repo](https://github.com/ConorWilliams/libfork) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18480)

#### bitsets-and-succinct

##### pasta::bit_vector  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++20 rank/select bit vector: 8% faster rank, 16.5% faster select than cs-poppy.

**Beats:** cs-poppy (Zhou, Andersen & Kaminsky, SEA'13 compact rank/select bit-vector structure) — In the SPIRE 2022 paper (arXiv:2206.01149), pasta-flat/pasta-poppy rank is up to 8% faster and pasta-flatSIMD select up to 16.5% faster than cs-poppy (Zhou, Andersen & Kaminsky, SEA'13) at matching ~3.51% space overhead, measured single-core on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X with GCC 10.2, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG. Not compared directly against any C++ stdlib facility, since none offers rank/select.

**How:** Uses a two-level (L1/L2) block metadata layout in the lineage of cs-poppy (Zhou, Andersen & Kaminsky, SEA'13), with 512-bit L2 blocks, tuned to hold the same ~3.51% space overhead while improving cache-friendliness of the 'flat' layout. The select path can locate the target L2 block with x86-64 SIMD intrinsics (FindL2FlatWith::INTRINSICS, compiled under __x86_64__) instead of linear or binary search over block summaries, which is where most of the select speedup comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Need succinct rank/select over a static, uncompressed bit vector (e.g., building an FM-index or other compact text index)
- Already using or evaluating cs-poppy-style compact rank/select structures and want the same space overhead with somewhat faster queries
- Target is x86-64 and can compile with -march=native to get the SIMD-accelerated select path
- Single-threaded/sequential query workload (paper's benchmarks are single-core)
- C++20 codebase where GPL-3.0 header-only vendoring is acceptable

**Skip it when:**
- Need a std::bitset/std::vector<bool>-compatible API — this is a separate type with its own construction and query interface, not a drop-in replacement
- License must be MIT/BSD-permissive — this is GPL-3.0, more restrictive than the sibling libraries in this category
- Rank-only workload where extra memory is acceptable — sdsl-v and rank9select answer rank faster but use 1.75-6.98x more space (per verification notes)
- Stuck on C++17 or earlier, or on a non-x86-64 platform where the SIMD select path is unavailable
- Need an actively maintained dependency — single-author project, last commit 2025-04-07, only 36 stars

**Integration:** header-only · tlx (github.com/tlx/tlx) and pasta-toolbox/utils, both pulled automatically via CMake FetchContent when building tests/benchmarks; no git submodules · C++20; CMake 3.25 to build tests/benchmarks via the provided presets (paper's benchmarks used GCC 10.2) · x86-64 for the SIMD-accelerated select path (FindL2FlatWith::INTRINSICS, gated on __x86_64__); a non-intrinsic linear/binary-search fallback exists for other architectures but is not the configuration benchmarked in the paper

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings (CRoaring, plf::bitset, better_bitset, BitLib, sul::dynamic_bitset) implement rank/select at all — they speed up direct std::bitset/std::vector<bool> operations like shifts, iteration, and set algebra. Pick pasta::bit_vector when the workload specifically needs succinct rank/select queries; for plain bit-twiddling workloads without that need, a sibling that benchmarks directly against std is the safer, lower-friction choice.

**Gotchas:**
- Support structures (e.g. FlatRankSelect) are constructed from an existing BitVector instance and query through that wrapper; build the bit vector first, then attach the rank/select structure you need
- Multiple rank/select variants exist (Rank/RankSelect, FlatRank/FlatRankSelect, WideRank/WideRankSelect) with WideRank explicitly meant for vectors up to 2^40 bits; the docs don't give a clear size crossover for picking one over another
- Building tests/benchmarks requires network access at configure time for CMake FetchContent to pull tlx and pasta-toolbox/utils
- The headline select speedup depends on -march=native and x86-64 SIMD intrinsics being enabled; behavior without that flag isn't the benchmarked configuration

**Status:** Maintenance is stale (single-author, last commit 2025-04-07, 36 stars), but it's header-only and small enough to read fully and vendor; GPL-3.0 licensing is the main adoption friction, not code quality.

[repo](https://github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01149)

#### k-mer-dictionaries

##### BLight  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Minimizer-partitioned, MPHF-based exact k-mer dictionary; indexes human k=31 at 22.3 bits/k-mer versus Pufferfish's 55.6.

**Beats:** Pufferfish — The BLight paper (Bioinformatics 37(18):2858) measured human k=31 on a Xeon E5-2420 at 1.9 GHz with 192 GB RAM under Ubuntu 16.04, with compiler and flags unstated. On 12 threads BLight built in 10 min with 7.4 GB peak and 22.3 bits/k-mer vs Pufferfish dense's 69 min, 27.4 GB and 55.59 bits/k-mer; querying all 2.5 billion reference k-mers took 1,748 s vs 1,799 s single-threaded and 155 s vs 655 s multi-threaded, and no std:: container, BBHash or other standalone MPHF was benchmarked.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked only against Pufferfish (and Squeakr/SRC, where it builds slower). The construction win needs 12 threads; single-thread queries are at parity on reference k-mers and slower on real reads (1,577 s vs 1,260 s).

**How:** K-mers are partitioned into 4^m buckets by minimizer (m=10 by default), and each run of consecutive k-mers that share a minimizer is stored once as a 2-bit-packed super-k-mer. Each partition gets a BBHash minimal perfect hash function. Per k-mer the index keeps only log2(super-k-mers in its bucket) bits that point to its super-k-mer, finds that super-k-mer's start with a BitMagic rank/select bitvector, and decodes it to check the hit, so answers are exact. The paper's breakdown is about 8-11 bits/k-mer for sequence, 4 for the MPHF, 5-13 for positions and under 1 for rank/select. Streaming queries cache the decoded super-k-mer and test the next query k-mers against it before touching the MPHF, and construction splits the input into 4^s temporary files that OpenMP threads process independently, which is why build and batch queries scale with cores.

**Use it when:**
- Static, duplicate-free k-mer set (k <= 32, canonical) from BCALM2 unitigs where RAM is the limit: the paper reports 22.3 bits/k-mer and 7.4 GB peak for the 2.5 billion human k-mers. It also built pine and axolotl (18.3 billion k-mers in 62.4 GB), where Pufferfish could not be built for lack of memory on a 192 GB machine.
- You need a dense k-mer-to-integer ID in [0, N) to index your own side arrays (counts, colors, flags) and you need exact negatives, not the arbitrary value a bare MPHF returns for absent keys.
- Batch-querying whole genomes or read files on a multi-core machine: all human reference k-mers took 155 s vs Pufferfish's 655 s with 12 threads (Table 2 labels the column 16T). The paper's Table 2 footnote says Pufferfish queries cannot benefit from multiple threads.
- Index build time matters and you have about 12 cores: 10 min for human vs 69 min for Pufferfish dense. BLight's single-thread build took 60 min, so the build win needs the threads.

**Skip it when:**
- Single-threaded querying: 1,748 s vs Pufferfish's 1,799 s on reference k-mers (parity), and 1,577 s vs 1,260 s on real reads (SRR5833294), so BLight is about 25% slower there.
- You want the smallest index or the fastest single-core lookups: in the SSHash paper's benchmark (i9-9940X, gcc 11.2, one core) BLight b=0 used 20.17 bits/k-mer vs 8.28-9.39 for SSHash, and streamed high-hit reads at 440 vs 253 ns/k-mer.
- Query streams that are mostly misses: the same benchmark measured 1,088 ns/k-mer for BLight on a low-hit stream vs 183 for canonical SSHash, and that paper notes BLight's query time degrades when most queries are negative.
- Sets that change, k > 32, or non-DNA keys: the index is static (rebuild to add k-mers), and the kmer type is uint64_t, with a commented-out __uint128_t typedef for k <= 64 that needs a recompile.
- Counting k-mer abundance from raw reads: in the paper's Table 4, BLight took 19:49 (hh:mm) vs 05:12 for SRC and 15:11 for Squeakr, and won only on peak memory (20.8 GB vs 44.2 and 185.4 GB).

**Integration:** source-drop · zlib and OpenMP; BBHash, BitMagic, LZ4, zstr and robin_hood are vendored in include/ and lz4/ · C++11 (the makefile uses g++ -std=c++11 -fopenmp); minimum GCC version not documented · x86-64 only in practice (SSSE3 _mm_shuffle_epi8 via <tmmintrin.h>; the makefile sets -msse4 -march=native); POSIX/Linux (setrlimit, pthread); macOS and Windows not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick BLight over SSHash or RSHash when build RAM is the tightest limit (the SSHash paper measured 7.5 GB peak to build human with BLight vs 15.4 GB for SSHash) or when you want OpenMP-parallel construction and batch-query helpers in a C++11 codebase that can accept AGPL. Otherwise SSHash (8.28-9.39 vs 20.17 bits/k-mer, 253 vs 440 ns/k-mer streaming in that benchmark) and RSHash, which its entry reports as faster than SSHash, are smaller, faster per core, MIT-licensed and still maintained.

**Gotchas:**
- Input must be 2-line FASTA (one sequence line per record; no multi-line FASTA or FASTQ, per snippet.cpp) with no duplicate k-mers. Construction encodes every character other than uppercase A/C/G as T, while queries map bases with (c/2)%4 (N becomes G), so soft-masked or N-containing input gives wrong answers without any error.
- construct_index needs a working directory that already exists and opens 4^s temporary files (256 by default), so raise ulimit -n. Failures such as a file that cannot be opened call exit() instead of throwing, and the library prints progress and index recaps to stdout.
- Building a second index in the same process segfaults (issue #10, open since 2022-02-17 with no reply).
- get_hashes_query returns MPHF values, not positions, and there is no ID-to-k-mer access call (only a full iterator). An index loaded from disk hard-codes 20 threads for the file_query_* helpers, and the destructor deletes any files named _out0.._out<4^s-1> in the current directory.

**Status:** Stale since 2024-07-06 (last commit was a BCALM2 parsing tweak), with 4 open issues including an unanswered segfault report and a libBlight packaging PR open since 2021. The core is about 1,400 lines of blight.cpp plus vendored headers, small enough to vendor, but AGPL-3.0 carries copyleft to programs that link it, including network services.

[repo](https://github.com/Malfoy/BLight) · [benchmark](https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/37/18/2858/6209734)

#### math-simd-linear-algebra

##### VDT (VectoriseD maTh)  `C++`  `LGPL-3.0-or-later`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Header-only Padé-polynomial libm replacements for exp/log/trig/asin-acos-atan/isqrt, auto-vectorizable, 1.3-13x faster scalar.

**Beats:** <cmath> (libm) — The refereed CHEP2013 paper (glibc 2.12 libm vs VDT v0.3.6, GCC 4.8.1, Intel Core i7-4770K) reports scalar double-precision speedups from ~1.3x (isqrt) to ~12.8x (exp), with AVX2+FMA-vectorized log reaching ~22x; the README's separate i7-3930K table shows smaller but consistent scalar gains (Exp 2.7x, Log 2.8x, Tan 3.7x) rising to 4-8x with SSE/AVX. Both sources agree that scalar single-precision expf/logf/isqrtf are slower than libm.

**How:** Each function is a Padé/minimax rational-polynomial approximation adapted from the Cephes math library, evaluated with a small fixed number of multiply-adds instead of libm's argument-reduction-and-table-lookup algorithms. The scalar code uses no intrinsics, so it auto-vectorizes under GCC/Clang/ICC into SSE/AVX/AVX2(+FMA) loops; the array (*_v) signatures make this explicit for the compiler and unlock the larger SIMD gains. Accuracy is deliberately relaxed (~0.1-0.5 average LSB difference from libm per the README's own table) to keep polynomial degree and branching low.

**Use it when:**
- Hot loops calling exp/log/sin/cos/tan/asin/acos/atan/atan2/isqrt millions of times where ~0.1-0.5 ULP error is acceptable, e.g. physics simulation and reconstruction code (VDT originated at CERN and is used in Geant4 and LHC experiment software).
- Code that can call the array (*_v) signatures or already auto-vectorizes, since SIMD gains (SSE/AVX/AVX2+FMA) are consistently larger than scalar gains in both the README table and the cited paper.
- x86-64 builds where you can pick SSE/AVX/AVX2/FMA at CMake configure time, or ARM builds via the NEON CMake option (though NEON is not exercised in the published benchmarks).
- Projects willing to vendor a small LGPL-3 header-only library and either call vdt:: functions directly or use the PRELOAD build to intercept an existing libm-calling binary without recompiling it.

**Skip it when:**
- Need bit-identical results to libm/std math (finance, reproducibility-critical or correctness-critical code) — VDT trades ~0.1-0.5 ULP accuracy for speed on every function.
- Building on Windows: issue #1 (open) reports it isn't compatible (__restrict__ vs __restrict, missing _USE_MATH_DEFINES) with no merged fix.
- Building on aarch64: default CMake option SSE=ON still passes -msse and breaks the build (issue #21, filed 2025-04-29, open, unresolved as of the last commit).
- Scalar single-precision expf/logf/isqrtf specifically — the record's own benchmark numbers show these particular scalar variants are slower than glibc libm.
- Teams that need active upstream support: last commit 2025-04-03, several issues open for years (CMake overwrites user CXX flags, clang linking error, Python 3.12 removed the imp module the Python scripts depend on).

**Integration:** header-only · none (optional Vc library integration via USE_VC CMake option) · GCC >=4.8, AppleClang >=5.0, Clang >=3.3, or ICC >=15.0 (enforced by CMakeLists.txt); C++11 is required only to build the optional DIAG benchmarking/unit-test tools, not to use the headers · x86-64 primarily (SSE on by default, AVX/AVX2/FMA opt-in via CMake flags); NEON is an opt-in CMake option for ARM but the default aarch64 build is currently broken by the SSE flag (issue #21); not Windows-compatible per issue #1

**Vs siblings:** Pick VDT over SLEEF or trigno_simd_cpp when you want one small header-only LGPL library covering the whole transcendental family (exp/log/trig/inverse-trig/isqrt) with a production track record in CERN/Geant4 physics code, rather than SLEEF's correctly-rounded (1-ulp) precision or trigno_simd_cpp's narrower sin/cos/tan-only scope; choose SLEEF instead when correct rounding matters more than raw speed.

**Gotchas:**
- fast_expf has a documented undefined-behavior bug (left shift of a negative value) for large negative inputs such as -163.48, caught by UBSan; open since 2019 (issue #10) with a proposed but unmerged fix.
- Default CMake option SSE=ON means a plain `cmake .` still emits -msse even on non-x86 targets, which currently breaks aarch64 builds (issue #21).
- Accuracy varies per function: the README's own table shows isqrt averaging ~0.45 LSB off libm, the largest deviation of any function in the library.
- CMake overwrites user-supplied CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS instead of appending to them (issue #8, open since 2018).

**Status:** Maintenance is stale (last commit 2025-04-03; multiple issues from 2016-2025 remain open, including a Windows-incompatibility report and an unfixed UB bug), but it's LGPL-3.0-or-later, header-only, and small enough to vendor; it's still cited in the repo description as used in CERN's Geant4 and LHC experiment software.

[repo](https://github.com/dpiparo/vdt) · [benchmark](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/513/5/052027)

#### minimal-perfect-hash-functions

##### ConsensusRecSplit  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Minimal perfect hash function close to the 1.443 bits/key bound; builds about 100x faster than RecSplit at lower space.

**Beats:** RecSplit — The authors' single-threaded benchmark (MPHF-Experiments, 100M random strings of 10-50 bytes, GCC 11.2 -O3 -march=native, Intel i7-11700) puts ConsensusRecSplit k=256, epsilon=0.1 at 1.578 bits/key and 248 ns/key build, against RecSplit l=12, b=2000 at 1.613 bits/key and 25,667 ns/key: about 103x faster construction at slightly lower space. For about the same build time as that RecSplit setting (30,245 ns/key), it reaches 1.444 bits/key. No standard-library baseline is involved, and the paper's '>350x' figure compares against bipartite ShockHash-RS at 1.489 bits/key, not RecSplit.

**How:** It keeps RecSplit's recursive splitting but uses only balanced 2-way splits and finds their seeds with Consensus (Combined Search and Encoding of Successful Seeds). Each split gets a fixed-width field in one bit stream, and its effective seed is the 64-bit window ending at that field, so it includes the bits of the seeds before it. A depth-first search backtracks when a later split has no working seed. This brings the overhead down to about epsilon bits per seed for O(1/epsilon) expected work, so build time grows linearly in 1/epsilon rather than exponentially as in RecSplit and ShockHash. First, a threshold-based minimal k-perfect hash function (k = 256-32768, with a FiPS fallback for bumped keys) sorts the keys into buckets of exactly k. That skips the expensive, cache-unfriendly top splits.

**Use it when:**
- Large static key sets where MPHF size is the main constraint and you want 1.44-1.53 bits/key, a range where earlier methods need 30-360x more build time per the paper's Table 1.
- As a replacement for RecSplit at roughly 1.6 bits/key: k=256, epsilon=0.1 gives 1.578 bits/key at 248 ns/key build (about 25 s for 100M keys), while RecSplit l=12 needs 25,667 ns/key for 1.613 bits/key.
- Build-once, query-many workloads that can pay for one single-threaded construction of seconds (k=256) up to about 50 minutes (k=32768, epsilon=0.0005, 100M keys) in the process that will run the queries.
- String keys, or 64-bit keys that are already uniformly hashed, on 64-bit Linux with GCC 12+ in a project that is GPL-3.0-compatible.
- Research and benchmarking of near-space-optimal perfect hashing: it is the reference implementation of arXiv 2502.05613.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-critical lookups. Queries take 140-217 ns on 100M keys, compared with 78-84 ns for bipartite ShockHash-Flat and 139-156 ns for RecSplit in the same table. PTHash reports 37-55 ns at about 3 bits/key in its own benchmark.
- You need to save the function and load it later. There is no serialization API, so every process must rebuild it, which takes up to an hour at the most compact settings.
- Proprietary or closed-source distribution. The license is plain GPL-3.0 with no runtime exception (unlike ShockHash), and the Util, FiPS and pasta bit_vector dependencies are also GPL-3.0.
- Fast or parallel builds at 2-3 bits/key. Construction is single-threaded, the paper leaves parallelization as future work, and it compares only against methods below 1.6 bits/key. At that space budget PTHash or SIMDRecSplit are the tested choices.
- Memory-constrained builds or production use that needs a maintained library. Build memory is not documented; the code keeps roughly 40 bytes per key of temporaries: 64-bit hashes, a 16-byte-per-key sort array and an unused copy of that array. The repo has 11 stars, no issues filed and no code commits since 2025-06-23.

**Integration:** header-only (CMake INTERFACE target added with add_subdirectory; no install or package-config rules) · Git submodules tlx (BSL-1.0, compiled), ips2ra (BSD-2-Clause), ByteHamster/Util (GPL-3.0, pulls pasta bit_vector, GPL-3.0) and FiPS (GPL-3.0). It also needs TBB, pthread and libatomic linked through ips2ra, even though ips2ra's parallel mode is off. At configure time, pasta bit_vector uses FetchContent to download pasta_utils and tlx from GitHub at origin/main. · C++20 (double non-type template parameter, std::span, std::bit_width), CMake 3.25+; CI builds with GCC 12, 13 and 14; the paper used GCC 11.2; Clang is not tested in CI · 64-bit Linux; CI runs only on x86-64 Ubuntu 24.04. No specific ISA is required: pasta uses BMI2 pdep only when it is enabled. The code assumes a 64-bit `unsigned long` (`~0ul` masks, `1ul << 63`), so Windows/MSVC (LLP64) is not expected to work.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when bits/key matters most. At about 1.5 bits/key it builds about 30x faster than bipartite ShockHash-RS from the ShockHash repo (584 vs 17,736 ns/key), and at 1.53-1.56 bits/key about 360x faster than SIMDRecSplit. Choose PTHash or bipartite ShockHash-Flat instead when query latency matters or 3 bits/key is fine, and ShockHash when you need its GPL runtime exception.

**Gotchas:**
- The object owns a raw `bucketingPhf` pointer and has a user-declared destructor but no copy or move operations. Copying it double-frees, and so does `std::move`, which falls back to the copy. Build it in place or on the heap, as the MPHF-Experiments harness does. The internal k-perfect hash function also never frees its rank/select structure.
- The `uint64_t` constructor uses the keys directly as hashes: the low 32 bits pick the bucket and the high 32 bits the threshold. Hash non-random integer keys first. String keys are reduced to a 64-bit MurmurHash64, and nothing checks for duplicates. Duplicate keys or 64-bit hash collisions (about 2.7% likely at 1B keys) can never be split, so the default level-wise search appears to loop forever. This is inferred from the code, not documented.
- `k` (a power of two) and `overhead` (epsilon) are template parameters. Every setting you want to try must be instantiated at compile time, as the benchmark's dispatch shows.
- The default level-wise constructor prints a timing line per tree level to `std::cout`, and the query-optimized one prints its tree size. The project adds `-march=native` only when it is the top-level CMake project.

**Status:** Stale research code from KIT: the last code commit is 2025-06-23 (the 2026-01-04 release tag points to it) and no issues have ever been filed. It builds with GCC 12-14 CI and can be vendored with add_subdirectory plus submodules, but only into GPL-3.0-compatible projects.

[repo](https://github.com/ByteHamster/ConsensusRecSplit) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05613)

##### Engineering Minimal/k-Perfect Hash Functions (stefanfred implementation)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Four minimal k-perfect hash functions; at k=10 threshold-based bumping builds 6.4x and queries 1.7x faster than cmph CHD.

**Beats:** CMPH CHD (cmph library, run as non-minimal k-perfect with load factor 0.97, because cmph CHD supports only non-minimal k-perfect hashing) and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping kPHF from CONSENSUS-RecSplit [30]; no BBHash, PTHash or 1-perfect RecSplit comparison — Paper Table 2 (ESA 2025) measures 100M random strings of length 10-50 with a single-threaded harness, GCC 11.2 -O3 -march=native, on an Intel i7-11700 running Rocky Linux 9.5. At k=10, Threshold-Based builds in 77 vs 495 ns/key and queries in 56 vs 96 ns against cmph CHD, which was run non-minimal at load factor 0.97 and is slightly smaller (0.627 vs 0.716 bits/key); Threshold-Based + Consensus beats CHD on all three axes (0.450 bits/key, 233 ns/key, 57 ns/query). CHD crashed at k=1000, and there are no k=1, BBHash/PTHash or std:: comparisons.

**How:** Threshold-based bumping hashes keys into ceil(n/(k*gamma)) overloaded bins (gamma > 1). Each bin stores a few-bit index into a small table of fingerprint thresholds, chosen to minimize expected empty slots under a gamma-distribution model, so most queries cost one bin hash and one comparison; bumped keys go to further layers, and a small FiPS 1-PHF plus an Elias-Fano list places the last few keys into leftover slots. Construction only radix-partitions keys by bin (ips2ra) and runs quickselect to find the k-th fingerprint instead of fully sorting, which the paper credits for being up to 50% faster to build than the next-best technique; optional 1-bit BuRR retrieval packing and CONSENSUS-coded thresholds trade some speed for space. The other three are k-perfect ports of known ideas: hash-and-displace with a k-specific optimal bucket-assignment function (CHD/PHOBIC style), RecSplit with leaves of size k, and PaCHash (an Elias-Fano predecessor search plus retrieval).

**Use it when:**
- You need a static set of string keys split into ceil(n/k) bins of exactly k keys. The paper's examples are a page index for an external-memory hash table, a completely filled bucketized in-memory table, and equal-size partitions for building 1-perfect hash functions.
- Large k (100-1000) where index size matters. At k=1000, Threshold-Based uses 0.010-0.011 bits/key (lower bound 0.006) with 44-45 ns/key construction and 24-25 ns queries on 100M keys.
- You currently use cmph CHD_PH in k-perfect mode. At k=10, Threshold-Based builds in 77 vs 495 ns/key and queries in 56 vs 96 ns, and it works at k=1000, where the authors report CHD crashes.
- Space-critical k=10 indexes. Threshold-Based + Consensus reaches 0.450 bits/key with 57 ns queries; k-RecSplit reaches 0.445 bits/key if 291 ns queries are acceptable.
- Benchmarking new kPHF designs: the repo's contenders/ and benchmarklib/ harness already wraps all constructions plus cmph CHD and the older ad-hoc threshold-based bumping.

**Skip it when:**
- You need an ordinary MPHF (k=1). No k=1 experiments exist, so use a 1-perfect sibling such as PTHash, PtrHash or ConsensusRecSplit.
- The key set changes, or the function must be persisted and reloaded. The structures are static, and none has save/load support (k-RecSplit's stream operators are compiled out with #if 0).
- You need a permissive license. The code is GPL-3.0, and its FiPS dependency is GPLv3 too.
- You use MSVC/Windows or a pre-C++23 toolchain. The targets require cxx_std_23, and the code relies on unsigned __int128, __builtin_ctzll and a 64-bit unsigned long (~0ul, 1ul << n). It was only tested on Linux x86-64.
- You need production maturity, non-string keys or a custom hasher. It is research code with 1 star, no releases and no unit tests beyond the benchmark's validity check. Keys must be std::string (hashed with SpookyHash), except that Threshold-Based also accepts pre-computed 128-bit hashes. Construction is single-threaded.

**Integration:** header-only (CMake add_subdirectory + git submodules; the ThresholdBasedBumping and PaCHash targets also build the SimpleRibbon/BuRR shared library) · Submodules: sux, ByteHamster/Util (with pasta-bit-vector), SimpleRibbon (BuRR, ips2ra, tlx), FiPS, gcem, tlx. cmph and ConsensusRecSplit are needed only for the benchmarks. HashDisplace.hpp includes a header by relative path from inside the simple-ribbon submodule. · C++23 (cxx_std_23), CMake 3.24+ (the SimpleRibbon, FiPS and Util submodules declare 3.25). Paper builds used GCC 11.2 with -O3 -march=native; spack.yaml pins GCC 14.2 and CMake 3.30. GCC/Clang only. · Tested only on x86-64 Linux (Intel i7-11700). There are no SIMD intrinsics in the kphf headers, but the code assumes LP64 and GCC/Clang extensions. -march=native is added only when the project is built top-level.

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling (PTHash, PtrHash, PHast, RecSplit, ConsensusRecSplit, ShockHash and others) is a 1-perfect MPHF, so pick this only when you need bins of exactly k>1 keys. Its Threshold-Based variant is the tuned successor of the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping in ConsensusRecSplit (1.293 -> 0.716 bits/key at k=10, 137 -> 56 ns queries), and k-RecSplit is the k>1 port of Sux RecSplit.

**Gotchas:**
- optimalThresholds.hpp and consensus.hpp define non-inline functions and a global (gammapdf, compute_thresholds_normalized, `uint64_t backtracks`). Including the threshold-based headers in more than one translation unit of a single binary therefore gives multiple-definition link errors, so confine them to one .cpp.
- Duplicate keys are never checked. k-RecSplit documents that duplicates make construction never return, and the other constructions do no deduplication either.
- Parameters must be tuned per k. The paper's Table 2 uses gamma=2.0 with 2^4-2^5 thresholds for k=10 and gamma=1.2 with 2^7-2^9 thresholds for k=1000. The benchmark binaries only instantiate k in {2, 4, 8, 10, 100, 1000}.
- k-PaCHash's build prints 'Num ribbon: ...' to stdout on every construction. Its bucket-scan loop also evaluates keys[offset] with offset == keys.size() after the last key, which is an out-of-bounds read (undefined behavior that sanitizers would flag).

**Status:** Frozen research code since the ESA 2025 paper (last commit 2025-07-03, 1 star, no issues, no releases, only a 'zenodo' tag). It is usable via CMake add_subdirectory with 8 submodules, but GPL-3.0 copyleft and unserializable structures limit production use.

[repo](https://github.com/stefanfred/engineering-k-perfect-hashing) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.20001)

##### LeMonHash  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Learned monotone minimal perfect hash (key to sorted rank): about 3-5 bits/key and 7-19x faster queries than trie-based MMPHFs.

**Beats:** Prior monotone MPHF implementations: the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Centroid Hollow Trie, Hollow Trie and Path Decomposed Trie (ot/path_decomposed_tries), plus the Belazzougui et al. Java implementations from Sux4J of the Hollow Trie Distributor, Hollow Trie, ZFast Trie, LCP, LCP 2-step, PaCo, VLLCP and VLPaCo — The ESA 2023 paper (arXiv v3) ran single-threaded on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 (2.3 GHz), with GCC 11.1.0 -O3 -march=native, and 5M random member queries per dataset. On 100M uniform 64-bit keys, LeMonHash (epsilon=31) answered 2.72M queries/s at 2.98 bits/key, against 0.35M at 4.61 for the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Hollow Trie (7.7x) and 0.18M at 4.54 for Sux4J's Java Hollow Trie (15.2x). On 800M osm keys it answered 1.34M/s at 4.42 bits/key, against 0.073M for Sux4J's HTDist (18.3x) and 0.19M for the C++ Hollow Trie (7.2x). The Java baselines ran on OpenJDK 17 after one unmeasured JIT warm-up, each experiment ran twice and was averaged, and no std:: container, binary search or non-monotone MPHF was measured. The paper's own Table 2 reports 1.85M queries/s for the same uniform configuration, so per-query cost depends on the harness.

**How:** Trie-based MMPHFs walk a trie; LeMonHash instead learns the key distribution. A PGM-index (an error-bounded piecewise-linear model, epsilon=31 by default) gives each key an approximate rank, which is used directly as its bucket index, so most buckets hold 0 or 1 keys. The start rank of each bucket is kept as a unary bit vector with a pasta select structure (2n+o(n) bits). Only keys that collide get a local rank stored, in one of ten BuRR (bumped ribbon retrieval) structures picked by ceil(log2 bucket size); the paper puts BuRR's space overhead below 1%. A query is a predecessor search over the PGM segments, one linear-model evaluation, one select and at most one retrieval lookup. That is a small, flat number of memory accesses, where Hollow and ZFast tries chase pointers down O(log u) levels. LeMonHash-VL applies the same scheme recursively to strings. It strips each node's common prefix and turns the next 64-bit chunk into a key, compressing the chunk through a per-node reduced alphabet. It finds child nodes through a PTHash MPHF and per-level partitioned Elias-Fano offset arrays.

**Use it when:**
- Static, sorted sets of 64-bit integers (IDs, positions, cell IDs, timestamps) where you need each key's rank but cannot afford to store the keys. The paper measured 2.6-3.0 bits/key on uniform, normal, exponential and 5gram data and 4.4-4.9 bits/key on osm and fb, against 4.1-6.0 bits/key for the Hollow-Trie family and 6.1-7.9 for PaCo and ZFast.
- Query-heavy rank lookups on large sets (100M-800M keys). Single-threaded on a 2014 Xeon it answers 1.3-2.7M queries/s: about 7-8x the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Hollow Trie and 12-21x the Sux4J Java Hollow Trie and HTDist, at the same or smaller space on every integer dataset except fb.
- Mapping a sorted key universe onto a dense value array while keeping locality. Consecutive keys land in consecutive slots, so range scans stay sequential. The paper notes this can make an MMPHF preferable to a plain MPHF for array indexing, because memory accesses in sorted order are cache-friendlier.
- Sorted string dictionaries (terms, k-mers) with LeMonHash-VL, when query speed matters more than the last 10-13% of space. On 35M web terms it answers 1.28M queries/s at 6.08 bits/key. The smallest competitor (HTDist) manages 0.09M/s at 5.40 bits/key, and the C++ Hollow Trie 0.35M/s at 5.84.
- Batch rebuilds where construction time counts. The default epsilon=31 integer build runs at 5.0-8.5 MKeys/s single-threaded (about 120-200 ns/key), up to 2x faster than the competitor with the next-best space.

**Skip it when:**
- You do not need sorted order. Every catalogued sibling is a non-monotone MPHF at about 1.5-3 bits/key, with catalogued query times in the tens of nanoseconds (on other hardware). In the paper's runs LeMonHash takes about 370-750 ns per integer query and 0.8-3 us per string query.
- Membership tests or changing key sets. Foreign keys get an arbitrary rank (there is no fingerprint), any insert means a full rebuild, and without serialization every process start rebuilds from the full in-memory key vector: 5-8.5 MKeys/s for integers, 2.3-2.7 MKeys/s for strings.
- Long URL-like strings, or when minimum space is the goal. On 106M URLs (average 105 bytes) LeMonHash-VL drops to 338K queries/s, and the C++ Centroid Hollow Trie is 18% faster there (399K/s at 8.36 vs 6.46 bits/key). On strings, LeMonHash-VL uses 10-13% more space than HTDist. On fb IDs, the Hollow tries and HTDist beat LeMonHash's 4.91 bits/key (4.50-4.84).
- Non-x86-64, non-GCC or non-Linux targets. support/util.h includes <immintrin.h> unconditionally, the string code assumes little-endian unaligned 64-bit loads, and CI covers only GCC 10-13 on x86-64 Ubuntu.
- Proprietary or permissively licensed products. LeMonHash is GPL-3.0 and links GPL-3.0 ByteHamster/Util.

**Integration:** header-only API (CMake INTERFACE target `LeMonHash`) that links small compiled shared libs: SimpleRibbon/BuRR, RibbonSorter and 4 sdsl-lite source files. It is consumed as a recursive git submodule via add_subdirectory; there are no install or package-config rules. · Git submodules: SimpleRibbon (Apache-2.0 BuRR wrapper, built as a shared lib, pulls ips2ra and tlx), ByteHamster/Util (GPL-3.0, pasta bit_vector, MurmurHash64), ds2i (partitioned Elias-Fano; its configuration.hpp uses boost::lexical_cast), sdsl-lite (bit utilities, partly compiled), PTHash (MIT, used by LeMonHash-VL for node lookup) and tlx. System: Boost (README requirement); CI also installs libtbb-dev. The PGM-index is re-implemented in-tree (include/bucket_mapping/support), not pulled as a dependency. · C++20 (cxx_std_20) and CMake 3.25+. The README says GCC 11 or later, but the 2026-09-13 CI run built successfully on GCC 10, 11, 12 and 13. Clang and MSVC are not tested. The paper used GCC 11.1.0. · x86-64 Linux as written. The integer variant pulls in <immintrin.h> through BucketOffsets.hpp -> support/util.h. bextr uses BMI when __BMI__ is defined and falls back otherwise. ds2i is configured with SUCCINCT_USE_INTRINSICS, described as 'available on all x86-64'. -march=native is added only when LeMonHash is the top-level CMake project. The bundled benchmarks need glibc (mallinfo2). ARM, macOS and Windows are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** All catalogued siblings (PTHash, PtrHash, RecSplit, ShockHash, SicHash, PHast and others) are non-monotone MPHFs, so pick LeMonHash only when the output must be the key's rank in sorted order: range scans over a rank-indexed array, or rank queries on a static set without storing it. If any bijection to [0,n) will do, PTHash or PtrHash (about 3 bits/key and 37-45 ns queries in their entries) or ShockHash or RecSplit (1.56-1.8 bits/key) beat LeMonHash's 2.6-4.9 bits/key and roughly 0.37-0.75 us per integer query, though those numbers come from different hardware.

**Gotchas:**
- Input must be sorted and duplicate-free, and the whole set must be in a std::vector. The integer constructor throws std::invalid_argument('Data not sorted or duplicates found'), but LeMonHashVL checks order only through debug asserts, so sort and deduplicate strings yourself.
- Do not copy or move a built object. SimpleRibbon's MultiRetrievalDataStructure owns raw SimpleRibbon* pointers and deletes them in a user-declared destructor, with no copy or move constructors. The implicit copy (which a move also falls back to) therefore creates two owners, and both delete the same pointers. Construct in place or behind new/unique_ptr, as the author's MMPHF-Experiments wrapper does.
- The defaults are the paper's tuned settings: LeMonHash<> uses SuccinctPGMBucketMapper<31>, and LeMonHashVL<> uses thresholds 128/128, alphabet reduction and UnalignedPGMBucketMapper<63>. epsilon=0 auto-tunes over 63/31/15 and roughly halves integer build speed (3.5 vs 6.5 MKeys/s on uniform keys) for little space gain. LinearBucketMapper and LeMonHashHeuristic only suit uniform data: on fb the linear mapper needs 34.35 bits/key and manages 0.8K queries/s.
- LeMonHashVL packs a node's common-prefix length into a 15-bit field and per-level offset indexes into 30 bits, and throws 'Increase offsetsOffsetBits' when the offsets overflow. Expect trouble with shared prefixes over 32 KB or with more than about 1B bucket offsets in one tree level. spaceBits() prints to stdout.

**Status:** The code has barely changed since 2023: dependency and CMake upgrades in 2024-2025 and a SimpleRibbon/BuRR submodule bump on 2026-09-13, with CI green on GCC 10-13. It has 32 stars and has never had an issue or PR filed. GPL-3.0 and the submodule-based build limit it to GPL-compatible projects.

[repo](https://github.com/ByteHamster/LeMonHash) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.11012)

##### PHOBIC-GPU  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Vulkan GPU builder for PHOBIC minimal perfect hash functions; builds about 62x faster than 8-thread CPU PHOBIC.

**Beats:** PHOBIC (CPU construction, part of jermp/pthash) — The authors' PHOBIC paper (arXiv 2404.18497, ESA 2024, Table 1) built MPHFs on 100M random 10-50 character strings. PHOBIC-GPU (RTX 3090 via Vulkan 1.3.236, plus 8 CPU threads) took 27 ns/key at lambda=9 with interleaved Rice coding (1.76 bits/key, 52 ns CPU query). The authors' own CPU PHOBIC took 1,781 ns/key with 8 threads and 9,171 ns/key with 1 thread on an i7-11700 (GCC 11.4.0 -O3 -march=native). The text calls this a 62x speedup (the table itself gives about 66x) and about 30x less energy (405 W vs 195 W draw). No std:: baseline is involved: this compares the same algorithm on a GPU and on a CPU.

**How:** It runs the PHOBIC algorithm: PTHash-style bucket placement with an optimized bucket-size distribution (OptBucketer), tiny partitions of about 2,048-2,500 keys, and interleaved coding of the seeds. Each partition maps to one Vulkan compute workgroup, and that partition's occupancy bitmap fits in fast shared memory. A per-partition counting-sort shader orders buckets by decreasing size. All threads in the workgroup then search seeds together with a single-loop version of the usual seed/key nested loop: a shared atomicAdd hands out the next candidate, and atomicMin keeps the smallest working seed, which avoids warp divergence. Seeds encode p = s*m + d (an additive displacement), so trying the next candidate only adds 1 to cached positions. The CPU uses OpenMP for the xxHash3-128 master hashing and the final Rice/Compact encoding.

**Use it when:**
- Rebuilding large MPHFs (the paper benchmarks 10^8 string keys) where build time dominates and a desktop GPU is idle: 27-28 ns/key vs 1,781 ns/key for 8-thread CPU PHOBIC at lambda=9.
- Space-efficient settings (lambda 9-14, about 1.67-1.76 bits/key) that are too slow to build on a CPU. For example, lambda=13 gives 1.68 bits/key at 560 ns/key on the GPU, and the paper says much larger lambda is not feasible on the CPU.
- Query-heavy lookup tables that need PTHash-class CPU query latency (37-52 ns) but GPU-speed builds. RecSplit-GPU builds equally fast but queries in 126-147 ns.
- Linux machines with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU that supports VK_KHR_maintenance4, where build energy matters: the paper measures about 30x less energy per build than the 8-thread CPU.

**Skip it when:**
- Small inputs or small lambda. Moving the keys to the GPU dominates there: Fig. 6 in the paper shows the GPU needs large n (many partitions) and large lambda to pay off.
- When you need faster queries. Queries run the same CPU code as PHOBIC, so only construction gets faster.
- When you need to save and load the function, build in external memory, or go past 2^32 keys. The MPHF class has no serialization, the key count is a uint32_t, and all keys are uploaded to the device at once (16 bytes/key for the key buffer alone). pthash covers these cases.
- Machines without a Vulkan GPU and driver. Only an Nvidia RTX 3090 on Linux was benchmarked, and CI only builds on Ubuntu 22.04 without running anything.
- Production use without in-house maintenance: this is research code with 4 stars, one merged PR, no issues filed, and GPL-3.0 copyleft.

**Integration:** shared lib · Vulkan SDK (libvulkan, headers, glslc shader compiler), OpenMP; git submodules xxHash, jermp/essentials, tlx (benchmark CLI only); bundled fastmod.h · C++17, CMake 3.19+, Vulkan 1.3 (shaders compiled with --target-env=vulkan1.3, SPIR-V 1.5); the paper used GCC 11.4.0 · Linux with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU that has VK_KHR_maintenance4 (prefers a discrete GPU; benchmarked only on an Nvidia RTX 3090); the query-side code is plain C++

**Vs siblings:** Choose this over PTHash, whose master branch now ships CPU PHOBIC as pthash::phobic, only when you have a Vulkan GPU and build time on about 10^8 keys dominates; PTHash gives the same query path plus serialization and multithreaded or external-memory builds. Choose it over GpuRecSplit (CUDA) when query latency matters: build speed is similar (27 vs 24 ns/key at about 1.8 bits/key) but CPU queries take 52 ns vs 126 ns; GpuRecSplit is the better choice below 1.6 bits/key (1.58 bits/key at 80 ns/key).

**Gotchas:**
- Compiled shaders are loaded at runtime from the relative path "shaders/<name>.comp.spv" under the current working directory, but the build writes them to ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/shaders. A process started from any other directory throws "failed to open file".
- The README says to link `PHOBIC-GPU`, but the CMake target is actually `GpuPTHash` (MPHF-Experiments links `GpuPTHash`).
- Debug builds (NDEBUG unset) turn on VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation and throw std::runtime_error if the layer is not installed. All Vulkan failures, including out-of-memory on the device, are reported as std::runtime_error.
- The example says the partition size should be tuned for your GPU (defaults: 2,048 in MPHFconfig, 2,500 in the paper). MPHF-Experiments has to `#undef MAX_BUCKET_SIZE` between including pthash.hpp and phobic_gpu_mphf.hpp.

**Status:** Stale research code: the last commit (2025-07-03) only edited the README, and the last code change was 2025-03-20. It has 4 stars and is GPL-3.0 (but CITATION.cff says AGPL-3.0-or-later). You can use it via CMake add_subdirectory, but expect to fix things yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/stefanfred/PHOBIC-GPU) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18497)

##### RecSplit (Sux C++ library)  `C++`  `GPL-3.0-or-later WITH GCC-exception-3.1`  `stale`  `Tier A`

Header-only RecSplit MPHF: 1.8 bits/key, smaller than CMPH's CHD and about 2x faster to build and query on 1e9 keys.

**Beats:** CMPH — In the PTHash authors' mphf_benchmark (Table 5 of the SIGIR'21 paper): 1e9 uniformly random 64-bit keys, one core of an i9-9900K, gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native. RecSplit l=8,b=100 built in 936 s at 1.80 bits/key with 204 ns lookups; CMPH's CHD took 1972-23746 s (lambda 4-6) for 2.01-2.17 bits/key with ~417 ns lookups. At 1e8 keys the same table shows a smaller build gap (92 s vs 121 s for CHD lambda=4; lookups 124 vs 204 ns). The harness pins a May 2020 sux commit (before the BMI2-detection fix that PR #16 says speeds queries by 10-20%) and builds CMPH through its own autotools configure.

**How:** Keys are hashed once to 128 bits with SpookyHash and bucketed, b keys per bucket on average (5 to 2000). Each bucket is split recursively: fanout 2 at the top, then fixed-size groups, down to leaves of at most LEAF_SIZE keys. At every node a brute-force search finds a seed that splits the keys exactly (at leaves, one that maps them bijectively). Only the seeds are stored, as Golomb-Rice codes whose parameters are tables computed at compile time, and a double Elias-Fano list gives each bucket's key offset and bit position. A lookup is therefore one Elias-Fano access plus a short walk down one bucket's tree, using multiply-shift range reduction and broadword select (BMI2 pdep/tzcnt when compiled for it). The RecSplit paper (ALENEX 2020) reports 1.56 bits/key this way, 8.3% above the 1.44 bits/key lower bound.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets of millions to billions of keys (URLs, k-mers, dictionary terms) that are built once and queried many times, where the MPHF must be small: about 1.8 bits/key at LEAF_SIZE=8, b=100, down to 1.56 bits/key at LEAF_SIZE=16, b=2000.
- Replacing CMPH's CHD in C++ code: on 1e9 random 64-bit keys RecSplit l=8,b=100 is smaller (1.80 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key), builds 2.1-25x faster and answers lookups in about half the time (204 vs ~417 ns).
- When you want to tune space against build time: LEAF_SIZE (a template parameter) and bucket size cover the range from 233 s at 2.95 bits/key (l=5, b=5) to 936 s at 1.80 bits/key (l=8, b=100) on 1e9 keys.
- Read-heavy services that query one built instance from many threads: operator() is const and has been thread-safe since 1.0.1.
- Linux servers with large key sets, where AllocType::TRANSHUGEPAGE or FORCEHUGEPAGE puts the structure on huge pages; switching takes one template argument.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency-bound lookups: about 200 ns/key at 1e9 keys in the PTHash paper's Table 5, against 37-64 ns for PTHash at 3-4 bits/key.
- When the build must be fast or parallel at very low space: this construction is single-threaded, and the GpuRecSplit README measures it at about 1.2 ms/key for l=16, b=2000 (1.56 bits/key), against 138 us/key for single-threaded SimdRecSplit.
- Dynamic sets or membership tests: the structure is immutable (any change means a full rebuild), and keys outside the set map to arbitrary valid indices (issue #21), so you must store your own fingerprints to reject them.
- Key sets that don't fit in RAM: this implementation holds all 128-bit hashes in memory (16 bytes/key, about 16 GB for 1e9 keys) and sorts them. The paper's external-memory construction is not implemented here.
- Windows/MSVC builds: the headers need POSIX sys/mman.h, GCC/Clang builtins and attributes, and variable-length arrays, and CI builds only on Ubuntu x86-64.

**Integration:** header-only · none (SpookyV2.hpp is bundled; googletest only for the test suite) · C++20 (std::span, since PR #23 in Oct 2024); GCC or Clang; __int128 support for more than 2^32 keys · POSIX. x86-64 has BMI/BMI2 fast paths with portable fallbacks, and an aarch64 build fix was merged in 2022 (PR #15). CI covers only Ubuntu 24.04. The PTHash mphf_benchmark harness disables RecSplit on __APPLE__.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you want the authors' small, dependency-free reference RecSplit that you can copy into an include path at about 1.8 bits/key. Take SimdRecSplit/GpuRecSplit for the same structure with 8-50x faster (and multi-threaded) construction, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit below about 1.6 bits/key, PTHash for 3-5.5x faster lookups at 3-4 bits/key, and emphf when 2.61 bits/key with a 374 s build at 1e9 keys fits better than RecSplit's 1.80 bits/936 s or 2.95 bits/233 s.

**Gotchas:**
- Duplicate keys make the constructor loop forever (documented in the header, and issue #20 was closed as won't-fix), so deduplicate first.
- The hash128_t constructor assumes uniformly random 128-bit hashes and sorts your span in place. Structured values such as hash128_t(0, i) overflow the fixed 3000-key bucket limit and segfault (issue #7). Hash integer keys first, e.g. with first_hash(&key, sizeof key) as mphf_benchmark does.
- Compile with -DNDEBUG: the code is 'heavily asserted', and without it the Elias-Fano constructor re-checks every bucket. Errors come as assert/abort, never exceptions: loading a file saved with another LEAF_SIZE calls abort(). The serialized format is raw host-endian binary with no version field.
- Header hygiene: 'using namespace std' inside sux::function, global macros (likely, unlikely, first_hash, skip_bits, ALLOW_UNALIGNED_READS) and a global SpookyHash class can collide with other code in a large codebase.

**Status:** Stale: the master branch is unchanged since October 2024 and the last release is 1.0.4 (June 2023). A May 2026 'bench' branch commit touches only Elias-Fano/select, not RecSplit. There are no open issues, and this is the algorithm authors' own header-only code under GPLv3 plus the GCC Runtime Library Exception ('use it everywhere, exactly like libstdc++'), though RecSplit.hpp still carries a leftover LGPLv3 paragraph, which is why GitHub reports NOASSERTION.

[repo](https://github.com/vigna/sux) · [benchmark](https://github.com/roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark/blob/main/README.md)

##### ShockHash  `C++`  `GPL-3.0 WITH GCC-exception-3.1`  `stale`  `Tier A`

C++ minimal perfect hash: RecSplit with cuckoo-hashing leaves, building 1.56-1.58 bits/key MPHFs 15-160x faster than RecSplit/SIMDRecSplit.

**Beats:** RecSplit — The paper's Table 1 (arXiv 2308.09561v2) measures 10M random strings of length 10-50, single-threaded, compiled with GCC 11.2.0 -O3 -march=native on an Intel i7-11700 with AVX-512, running SIMDShockHash with rotation fitting. At ~1.56 bits/key, ShockHash-RS n=39 builds at 1,805 ns/key against SIMDRecSplit's 137,902 ns/key (~76x). At ~1.585 bits/key, n=30 builds at 787 ns/key against sux RecSplit's 125,521 ns/key (~160x), but only ~15x against SIMDRecSplit's 11,749 ns/key. Queries are 114-118 ns against 97-108 ns.

**How:** It keeps RecSplit's recursive splitting tree but replaces the brute-force bijection search in each leaf (about e^n seed trials) with ShockHash ('small, heavily overloaded cuckoo hash tables'): each seed gives every key two candidate cells in an n-cell table, and the seed is accepted if the random graph is a pseudoforest, meaning the table can be filled completely by cuckoo insertion. A 1-bit BuRR ribbon retrieval structure records which of the two cells each key uses, and this cuts the expected trials to (e/2)^n·poly(n), almost 2^n fewer, so leaves can have n=30-58 instead of RecSplit's ~8-16. Most seeds are rejected early by a bit-mask filter that checks every cell is hit; the filter runs in registers with AVX2/AVX-512 SIMD, and rotation fitting tries n cyclic rotations of half the keys per hash evaluation.

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets (millions to hundreds of millions of string keys) where the MPHF must sit close to the 1.44 bits/key lower bound. Table 1 configurations reach 1.52-1.58 bits/key.
- You already use RecSplit or SIMDRecSplit at b=2000 with leaf 14-16 and build time is the bottleneck. At matched space, ShockHash-RS builds in 787-1,805 ns/key; RecSplit and SIMDRecSplit take 11,749-137,902 ns/key.
- Processes that build the function once and keep it in RAM, where a ~115 ns query is acceptable. For example, 10M keys with n=30, b=2000 is about 8 s of single-threaded construction.
- x86-64 Linux with GCC 11+ and AVX2 or AVX-512, using SIMDShockHash with rotation fitting. This is the configuration the paper measured.
- To go below ~1.52 bits/key, use `ShockHash2` (bipartite ShockHash, arXiv 2310.14959) from the same repo. Its abstract reports 1.489 bits/key for 10M keys in about half an hour.

**Skip it when:**
- Lookup latency is the constraint. In the same Table 1, queries take 114-118 ns; PTHash takes 20-34 ns and FMPHGO 53-69 ns, at 2.2-4.4 bits/key.
- You need to save the function to disk and load it later. ShockHash, SIMDShockHash and ShockHash2 have no serialization API (sux RecSplit has `operator<<`/`operator>>`), so every run must rebuild.
- Dynamic key sets, or code that must detect foreign keys. The function is static and returns an arbitrary index for keys it was not built on, so you need a separate key or fingerprint store.
- Clang, MSVC, Windows, macOS or ARM toolchains. CI covers only GCC 11/12/13 on Ubuntu, the code uses `<experimental/simd>`, raw x86 intrinsics in the SIMD path and `1ul` shifts of up to 60 bits, and CMake links Intel TBB.
